subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REPORTED COMPLAINT AS TO DOCKING FACILITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the statement made by Sir Colin Anderson, a director of the P. & O. line, as reported in the Vancouver press on February 3 and 4 on the occasion of the visit of the new P. & O. liner Oriana, to the effect that docking facilities in Vancouver are "among the poorest in the world", can the minister comment on this statement and indicate whether he will have the national harbours board investigate this condition?

subtopic: VANCOUVER
subsubtopic: REPORTED COMPLAINT AS TO DOCKING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read the press comment on the visit of the Oriana, which appears to indicate that Sir Colin Anderson's statement was directed to criticism of the harbour facilities in general. We have assurance from Sir Colin that he was referring specifically to the passenger reception facilities on the particular pier at which the ship was docked, which incidentally is a privately owned facility.
Although it has not been requested to provide such accommodation, the national harbours board has been for some time interested in the possible provision of a deep sea passenger terminal in the port of Vancouver, and has approached local and Pacific coast shipping agents handling passengers with a view to modifying one of its existing piers for this purpose. Agents and owners have stated a preference for berthing their ships in a location where they may be readily observed and visited most conveniently by the largest number of people possible, and none of the existing board facilities meet these requirements.
It should be kept in mind that to date deep sea passenger traffic through the port of Vancouver numbers well under 20,000 passengers 90205-6-1141
Inquiries of the Ministry annually, a substantial number of whom arrive and depart on freighters and who consequently would not use a terminal created for the exclusive use of passengers. This circumstance imposes obvious and severe economic limitations on the construction of such a terminal. However, I can assure my hon. friend that this is a matter which is being given consideration by the Vancouver harbour planning committee.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. PLAN FOR PEACE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is Canada one of the countries that has been consulted by the United States with regard to its plan to bring peace in the Congo and preserve the integrity of the Congo, as announced by the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs yesterday in Washington?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secreiary of Siaie for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. PLAN FOR PEACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government welcomes the United States initiative. The new policy contains a number of important elements which Canada has always believed were necessary to a solution of the crisis in the Congo. For example, it implies an attitude of impartiality in the
Inquiries of the Ministry internal political affairs of the Congo. This is the attitude which Canada has maintained from the outset of the crisis, consistent with Canadian membership on the secretary general's advisory committee for the Congo and our participation in the force. As the hon. member knows, Canada is one of the 18 nations represented on this Congo committee, all of them having substantial forces in the Congo.
It implies a willingness to face realistically the fact that there are a number of contending political elements in the Congo, each with a certain strength, which cannot simply be wished out of existence. In the Congo debate in the general assembly just before Christmas the Canadian spokesman, namely the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who is my parliamentary secretary, argued that no political solution was likely to be viable in the Congo which did not take these facts realistically into account.
The new United States policy will also presumably be an important factor in meeting the request which the secretary general once again made to the security council on February 1 for a clarification of his mandate. On this point also the parliamentary secretary, in defining Canada's Congo policy to the general assembly in December, pointed out that Canada believed the mandate should be properly defined and that member states could hardly complain at the way in which the secretary general carried out his responsibilities so long as the general assembly was unable itself to agree on what the role of the United Nations should be and left the task of interpretation to the secretary general.
There may now be grounds for hope that some of the limitations on past United Nations action in the Congo can be corrected. I sincerely trust that this will be the outcome of recent developments and the current security council debate. The Canadian government will continue to advocate and support all measures which are designed to strengthen the position of the secretary general and are consistent with a policy of strict impartiality in Congolese internal affairs.
In this way we believe United Nations influence in the Congo can effectively be brought to bear in order to assist the Congolese to resolve problems which are essentially their own.

subtopic: RADIO AND TELEVISION TECHNICIANS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate inquired on February 2 with reference to advertisements appearing in British newspapers seeking radio and television technicians for employment in Canada. Reference was made to these in a news dispatch appearing in the Telegram of Tuesday, January 31. When I saw this news dispatch I immediately initiated inquiries of our London office requesting all available information as to the details of the advertisements reportedly appearing in the London Daily Mail and other newspapers.
We have not yet received full details on this matter from our London office, but I can assure the hon. member that the advertisements in question were not placed with the advance knowledge or approval of

this department. We have, of course, no means of controlling the placing of advertisements by private concerns in British newspapers.
When requests of this kind are received from employers in Canada our practice is to refer them to the national employment service, which endeavours first of all to fill the order from available applicants in Canada. Only if it is established that persons with the required qualifications are not available in Canada does the national employment service refer the order for completion to its overseas office in London.
Employers who do not follow this practice but who, instead, advertise directly in overseas newspapers can have no assurance that candidates recruited directly by them without clearance with the N.E.S. will be allowed to come forward to Canada. All such applications are dealt with in accordance with section 20(a) of the regulations, which provides that a British subject by birth or naturalization in the United Kingdom must first establish as a condition of his entry to Canada that he has sufficient means to maintain himself in Canada until he has secured employment therein. If the conditions laid down in the regulations are met the applicant is, of course, allowed to proceed.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON REPORTED U.S. ORDER RESPECTING AID SHIPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Peterborough asked
Pension Act
me a question concerning a ruling made by the international co-operation administration, which is a United States government agency that channels foreign aid and which ruled that effective February 1, freight will be paid only on aid cargoes moving in United States ships. I now have an answer to that question, which is as follows.
Under general United States legislation the international co-operation administration has been required to ship at least 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of commodities purchased under its programs on United States privately owned commercial vessels. By a recent order the United States international co-operation administration announced that ocean shipping costs of all commodities, materials and equipment procured from mutual security program funds shall be eligible for I.C.A. financing only if transported on United States flag vessels except-and this exception, I think, is important-where foreign flag vessels are required to ensure timely delivery of merchandise and provided that such exceptions receive prior approval from the international co-operation administration in Washington.
It is hoped that these exemptions will go some way to meet the concern of the great lakes ports. I understand that the international co-operation administration intends to hold hearings on this order and to entertain all reasonable requests for exemptions on contracts that would be jeopardized by the new regulations.
The Canadian embassy in Washington is now exploring the situation which is still somewhat unclear. I shall report to the house further should this be warranted. I think the concern was that this might result in a decrease in shipping through the seaway in favour of shipping from the east coast ports of United States, but our belief is that this will not be the effect of the ruling. However, we shall be very glad to keep in touch with that development.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, December 12, 1960, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependents; to permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a disabled veteran of the first great war, an honorary

Pension Act
member of the War Amputations of Canada, and one who has carried his disability for many years it gives me great satisfaction to take part in the discussion of this resolution. November 17, 1960 must have been a red letter day which stirred the hearts of disabled veterans and their dependents when hearing the speech from the throne in which our beloved Governor General included the following statement:
Amendments to the Pension Act will be recommended which will include substantial increases in the pensions payable to veterans or their dependents.
Throughout the years the War Amputations of Canada, the Canadian Legion, the Army, Navy and Air Force association, the Royal Canadian Air Force association, the Polish legion, the naval veterans association and others have placed before the veterans affairs committee and our government amendments to the Pension Act and other worth-while legislation concerning their disabled comrades of world wars I and II and Korea. May I on behalf of these comrades express our thanks to the government, the veterans affairs committee, the Canadian pension commission and the Department of Veterans Affairs for their support in bringing about from time to time better conditions for those who gave so much at a time when their country was in urgent need of their devotion to duty.
It is a privilege for me to congratulate the former minister of veterans affairs, Hon. Alfred Brooks, on his appointment to the other place. This hon. gentleman throughout the years has been a real friend of all veterans, and his untiring efforts for the welfare of thousands of Canadians will long linger in our thoughts.
I understand that the total number of pensioners under the Pension Act as at December 31, 1959 was 185,536, as compared with 195,635 in 1950. This decrease is mainly due to the sad fact that world war I pensioners are steadily passing away. On the other hand the number of world war II pensioners has increased from 88,233 in 1947 to 122,296 in 1959, an increase of 34,063. It is interesting to note in regard to this group that the number of children in respect of whom additional pension is being paid is 176,409, an increase of 54,759 since 1947.
These figures were supplied by Mr. T. D. Anderson, chairman of the Canadian pension commission, to the veterans affairs committee on April 7, 1960. As these figures are placed before us we realize that in a few short years many of the disabled veterans of world war I will not be with us, and that time is also running out for many of our world war II and Korean war pensioners. At the amputations

convention last year, tribute was paid to 130 pensioners who had died in the previous two years.
The people of Canada have been very sympathetic toward our veterans, especially the disabled. Canada's military performance in the two world wars and Korea is one of the chief reasons for the growth of her prestige and influence in world affairs. Canadian people realize that Canadians fought bravely and effectively in two wars and Korea, and that we had to fight these wars at such great cost. Part of this cost was paid by many in one grim payment, life itself. Others like myself and many with more serious disabilities are still paying in day by day instalments which will continue for the remainder of our lives.
The people of our country well understand the determination shown by our disabled veterans in obtaining and holding gainful employment despite their disabilities. We should, however, recognize that these people never know from day to day how long they will be able to continue working, particularly as they grow older and their disabilities become more difficult to bear. The courage of our veterans has never been questioned, be it in war, in daily routine or in recreation. Each year the amputees of Toronto, Hamilton and the Waterloo-Wellington branch enjoy a get together at which a softball tournament is arranged. Those participating must be amputees. Each player must run and bat for himself. My position has been that of pitching, which sometimes takes in 10 innings and two games. I could go on and mention many fine players despite their handicap?
Our greatest competitor under these conditions has been veteran Ed Wilkie of Kitchener, a triple amputee who lost both legs and one arm. His performance has been the talk of our community. He bats with one hand, walks to first base and, in stealing second, if late he will slide into that base. Of course this causes a delay in the game as he requires a few minutes to adjust his harness and pull himself together. I merely mention this to show that his splendid fortitude is an example to all of us who are more fortunate, and represents the challenging sense of determination. Men of his spirit are the backbone of our country. Yes, such veterans are contributing more and more to the economic, social and political life of Canada, and will continue to do so in future years.
Under the leadership of our former minister of veterans affairs our government has brought about important improvements during the past number of years. Some of these include amendments to the Veterans Insurance Act under which benefits are now available until September 30, 1962, after which all eligibility

ceases. I understand that all possible means to publicize this fact have been used. Amendments to this act, along with Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act, have given valuable security to the dependants of many of our comrades. Much could be said of the amendments to the Children of War Dead Education Assistance Act. Over 1,800 children have been approved for educational assistance under this act up to the present time. This could be one of the finest investments that our government has ever made.
The changes in the Veterans Rehabilitation Act were largely administrative, and the changes in the War Service Grants Act dealt with re-establishment credits. The most important one could be the extension of the period of eligibility for benefits to September 30, 1962 or, in the case of Korean veterans, 15 years after discharge. The amendments to the Veterans' Land Act extended to those who needed it; the principle of supervised farms and substantial amounts of additional capital through which they will be able to extend their farm businesses and improve their net returns. Another change which I believe pleased all veterans was the decision to pay an annuity of $300 to all holders of the Victoria Cross who won this highly prized award while serving with the Canadian forces in world war II or subsequently.
Hospitalization and medical treatment are becoming more and more necessary. With this in mind our government have completed or started, or have now in the planning stage, various hospital projects. I understand that a new 300-bed wing at Deer Lodge hospital, St. James, Manitoba, was completed during the summer of 1958, and is now making a great contribution toward the welfare of veterans. Shaughnessy hospital at Vancouver officially opened a new 314-bed wing last year. I had the privilege of visiting this hospital some years ago, and was impressed with its location and the service extended to those comrades.
After the first war in 1919 I entered Westminster hospital, London, Ontario. Improvements have been made to this hospital from year to year, and construction started last year on a new wing which will accommodate 300 more veterans. The Queen Mary Veterans hospital in Montreal, Ste. Anne's Veterans hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, and St. John's General at St. John's, Newfoundland, will be modernized at considerable cost. These improvements demonstrate that our government is intensely interested in the welfare of all veterans, especially those who are in need of medical care.
The War Veterans Allowance Act has been amended on several occasions, and in one instance consideration was extended to the
Pension Act
widows of recipients of those benefits which is not extended to the widows of those receiving benefits under the Pension Act. Upon the death of a married recipient of war veteran's allowance, his widow receives allowance at the full married rate for one year following his death, as she should. The widow of a person pensioned under the Pension Act does not receive any such supplementary benefits. This should be changed. This point was brought up by me in my address during the discussion of the veterans affairs estimates in July of last year. Therefore I recommend again that widows of those pensioned under the Pension Act at the rate of 50 per cent or more should receive the full married rate of compensation in effect at the time of the death of the pensioner for a period of not less than one year following such death.
Another point which I brought up at that time, and which has given others and myself much concern, was the continuation of the allowance after the death of a pensioner in receipt of a pension of less than 50 per cent. The present legislation reads:
In the case of those in receipt of less than 50 per cent at the time of death and whose death is not established as due to pensionable disabilities, no pension or allowance is paid.
In order to avoid further hardships, which have been brought to my attention on numerous occasions by widows in financial difficulties, I suggest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the government that the allowances in respect of wives and dependants being paid to the pensioner at less than 50 per cent at the time of death be continued to the widow and such dependants as long as they remain eligible as otherwise provided under the act. Perhaps we should also use the plan that is now being used for the widow of a pensioner who has a pension of 50 per cent or over.
Our government and the Department of Veterans Affairs are continually working on improvements for our limb and arm amputees. Recently Messrs. Butler and Mc-Lachan, close friends of mine and leg amputees of the second world war, journeyed to the United States where they invested in a Hydra-Cadence artificial limb. Although these limbs are in the trial stages as far as Canada is concerned, the facility of movement in the walking of these gentlemen has improved over 50 per cent. This has been my personal observation. I understand that considerable progress is being made in the development of this Hydra-Cadence limb, and that plans are under way for the Department of Veterans Affairs to obtain some of these units for trial use. This is commendable, and our gratitude for such a move is extended

Pension Act
to Dr. Crawford and his staff. I believe these limbs may be successful, and I am hoping that future tests may substantiate my remarks.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, this week Canada will observe white cane week. We as Canadians have always supported any worthwhile cause. With that in mind, I hope our financial efforts will be substantial. Among those who carry the white cane are quite a few of our comrades from world wars I and II. These veterans, along with the paraplegic cases and other 100 per cent pensioners, especially those living in the urban areas where the cost of living is high and who have disabilities in regard to earning power, are encountering many financial difficulties. May I recommend to the Minister of Veterans Affairs that when pension adjustments are forthcoming we make certain that the 100 per cent pensioner will not experience any financial worries in addition to his physical handicap. Let us be more generous to the 100 per cent pensioner who in most cases is unable to work because of his physical disability.
I believe that most Canadians have been satisfied with the governmental legislative programs which have safeguarded the welfare of our country's veterans. I believe too that over the years the presentations made by the different veterans organizations have been both reasonable and realistic. I feel sure that our Minister of Veterans Affairs and his department, the government and the veterans affairs committee will, when considering amendments to the Pension Act, realize the great importance of these amendments from the point of view of substantial increases in pension payments to veterans and their dependants.
It has been a real pleasure for me to be associated with my colleagues on the veterans affairs committee, and I wish to commend them for their untiring efforts and sincere deliberations on those important questions that pertain to the welfare of all veterans. Finally may I extend my sincere congratulations to our new Minister of Veterans Affairs. His distinguished war service and knowledge of veterans affairs will be of great value in filling this important governmental post. I extend to him my best wishes for his future success.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by expressing my congratulations to the minister on taking over this very important portfolio. I should like to take this opportunity to thank him publicly for the personal interest he has taken in those problems of veterans which I have already brought to his attention. I should also like to join with
[Mr. Weichel.l
all those who have paid tribute to the former minister of veterans affairs, who has now departed for the more serene atmosphere of the other place. Colonel the Hon. Alfred Brooks served on the veterans affairs committee for approximately 25 years, and we always found that when it was a matter of the problem of our veterans he had a very sympathetic heart. I am sure the new minister is determined to continue in that tradition.
As recorded on pages 734 to 736 of Hansard, the minister in introducing the resolution outlined several of the proposed amendments, the chief one of which will increase the rates of disability pensions and supplementary pensions to disabled veterans and their dependants, and will also make supplementary payments available to veterans outside of Canada. The minister also listed other increases such as the increase in the grant for burial expenses, the increase in the rates of children's allowances, and an amendment which will permit children in receipt of pension allowances to have them continued until the end of the month instead of being cut off on their birthday. This small additional allowance will be an acceptable birthday gift, but as the minister told us it will not amount to any very great financial assistance because it is being introduced mainly for the purpose of simplifying administration. The minister also mentioned that payments to children will be made equal for each child rather than being on an escalator scale, and that the payment to each child will be a little better than the present average.
We also welcome the amendment the minister has indicated he proposes to introduce with respect to widowers who have to hire someone, an older sister, an aunt or some other relative, to look after the children when the mother has passed away. This is a very welcome measure and will also serve to take care of the problem of orphans, which I think has been a difficulty up to the present time. All these measures are welcome.
At this stage we are discussing the principle of these measures, and since the principle is to help our veterans we are heartily in accord with it. Before we can criticize the minister's legislation we will have to have the bill before us to enable us to see how it measures up to the recommendations that have been made from time to time by members of the house and by representatives of the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations.
I was very glad to read the minister's statement, found on page 735 of Hansard, with regard to Canadian citizens who served in an allied force during world war I or II. This amendment will enable them to have the pensions they receive from the allied

government supplemented up to the Canadian rate. In short, this measure will put those Canadians who served in an allied force on the same footing as Newfoundland veterans. We have not been satisfied, of course, with that status, and it is a matter of disappointment that the minister made no reference to the position of Newfoundland veterans when he introduced the resolution.
We have always maintained that our veterans should be regarded as though they had served in Her Majesty's Canadian forces. That status was outlined in the terms of union. We have heard a great deal about the terms of union and one of them, term 29, has received extensive publicity. But there were more than 29 terms in the terms of union. Actually there were 50 terms, and in addition there was a schedule which outlined the federal districts in the province of Newfoundland. The term that applies to Newfoundland veterans is term 38, and I should like to put it on the record at this time. Term 38 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada is headed "Veterans" and reads as follows:
Canada will make available to Newfoundland veterans the following benefits, on the same basis as they are from time to time available to Canadian veterans, as if the Newfoundland veterans had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces, namely-
Then there follow a number of paragraphs setting forth the various benefits. Paragraph (a) deals with the War Veterans Allowance Act; paragraph (b) with the Pension Act; paragraph (c) with the Veterans' Land Act; paragraph (d) with re-establishment credits; paragraph (e) with vocational and educational training and paragraph (f) with the Veterans Rehabilitation Act. I should like to quote in full paragraph (b), which has to do with the Pension Act as it would apply to the Newfoundland veteran. This paragraph reads:
Canada will assume as from the date of union the Newfoundland pension liability in respect of the first world war, and in respect of the second world war Canada will assume as from the date of union the cost of supplementing disability and dependents' pensions paid by the government of the United Kingdom or an allied country to Newfoundland veterans up to the level of the Canadian rates of pensions, and, in addition, Canada will pay pensions arising from disabilities that are pensionable under Canadian law but not pensionable either under the laws of the United Kingdom or under the laws of an allied country;
So far as the Newfoundland veterans are concerned, they fall into four categories. In the first category come veterans of the first world war, and in that respect there is no problem. The other three categories have to do with veterans of world war II. Category 1 would be the veterans who were already in receipt of pensions from the United
Pension Act
Kingdom. Evidently those pensions would now be supplemented up to the prevailing Canadian rates, and that is quite all right. Category 2 would include Newfoundland veterans who had applied for British pensions and had been refused. Now these veterans would be eligible to apply to the Canadian pension commission for a pension and Canada would pay the pension according to this provision:
-in addition, Canada will pay pensions arising from disabilities that are pensionable under Canadian law but not pensionable either under the laws of the United Kingdom or under the laws of an allied country;
The veteran who had been turned down would be eligible to try again with the Canadian pension commission. With respect to the third category, this would include new applicants, people who had never applied to the United Kingdom. These veterans were to be treated, according to term 38, as if the Newfoundland veteran had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces. This is the plain wording of term 38, and term 38 is part of the British North America Act. It is part of our constitution and certainly should override any other legislation. Any legislation pertaining to veterans should be interpreted in the light of what term 38 says.
This has not happened. In so far as new applicants are concerned, they have not been treated as though they had served in Her Majesty's Canadian forces. They have been required to submit their applications to the British ministry of pensions just as they did before confederation. Now, no person who served in the Canadian forces has to apply to the British ministry of pensions, wait six or seven months to have his claim processed, and then find out whether or not he is going to get something. The veteran would then have to go to the Canadian pension commission and go through all that procedure again to get the pension supplemented if he were successful in getting a pension. The words of term 38 could not be clearer. They say that the benefits will be made available on the same basis as if the Newfoundland veteran had served in Her Majesty's Canadian forces. This provision relates to new applications.
We are glad to see that other Canadians who were getting pensions from allied governments are now to have their pensions supplemented; that is a good thing. However, we point out that, so far as Newfoundland is concerned, our case is different. These Canadians who were domiciled in Canada by-passed the Canadian forces. They did not have to go across to England or France to join up with the British forces; there were forces here in Canada that they could have joined. If they deliberately chose to by-pass the Canadian forces and enlist in the forces of another country, that was their choice. I do not believe

Pension Act
their claim is so strong, although I am glad to see they are being given consideration. I think that is a good measure, and I support it.
This is not the case with Newfoundland. The Newfoundland veteran did not by-pass the Canadian forces. He had no choice but to join the imperial forces, because we came under the imperial war measures act. Term 38, which I just quoted, takes care of that.
I know that hon. members will say, why has all this time passed and nothing been done about it? This is a fair question. Nothing has been done about it because we did not know about it until 1955 or 1956. We did not get any complaints from the veterans. I suppose one of the reasons we did not get complaints was that the average veteran did not know about term 38. He did not know the actual wording of it. It was only when we began to get complaints about long delays being experienced in the British ministry of pensions that we began to dig into this question. It was only four or five years ago that I became aware of this problem myself, since I had to dig into it. The point is that it has been brought before the house on several occasions.
The former minister of veterans affairs acknowledged this problem, and I should like to read something he said in that regard on December 19, 1957, as recorded on page 2632 of Hansard. I had outlined the same problem to him as I have here today, and in reply the minister said this:
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo with reference to Newfoundland veterans, I think there is a real case there and I am very much surprised that the problem of the Newfoundland veteran has not been dealt with before this time.
Then further down the page we find this; I am not going to quote the whole paragraph:
Any veteran who is a Canadian, whether he comes from Newfoundland or from any other part of Canada, should receive exactly the same treatment as that received by other Canadian veterans. That is my opinion and I think that would be the opinion of a veterans committee which might review the matter. I can assure the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that it will be given every consideration.
Well, those remarks were made on December 19, 1957. We come now to December 12, 1960 and we still find nothing in the minister's statement that gives us any encouragement to believe that this problem is going to be dealt with at all. I submit to the minister that perhaps legislation is not required to deal with it because it is a matter of interpretation. I noted that, as reported at page 736 of Hansard, the minister made this statement:
In some instances, the act and the interpretation of the act have limited the activities of the pension commission, and in the revision that is now going on it is our hope that some of the sections

which have hindered the commission from time to time may be altered so that its work may become more effective.
I do not know whether there are any sections of the act that are hindering the Canadian pension commission from implementing term 38 as I have quoted it here today. But if it is a matter of interpretation, certainly term 38 is clear. I do not see how it can be put in clearer language. That was a definite commitment of the parliament of Canada to the people and to the veterans of Newfoundland. We are just asking that it be implemented even at this late date. As I said, possibly it is just a matter of changing the interpretation.
Toward the end of the resolution itself I note that there is a rather curious clause. A part of this resolution is going to introduce an amendment for the following purpose:
-to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners-*
The minister did not explain what that language meant when he spoke. When he replies I hope he will clear up any mystery that may be hidden in these words. I am fully in agreement that there should be provision for appeals from the decisions of the pension commission, but I think it should apply with regard to every commission and not merely the former pension commission. I think every board of pension commissioners are sometimes going to make mistakes. I believe there should be a right of appeal, and I think the right of appeal should not be confined merely to decisions of the former board of pension commissioners.
Returning to the problem of the status of the Newfoundland veteran, I have quoted previously, and perhaps I might quote again to the new minister, a precedent. If he will look back over his records he will find a precedent which I think could be used to clear up the situation in regard to Newfoundland veterans. That precedent arises out of a situation which arose during world war II. During world war II there was a time when Britain was short of flyers to man her aeroplanes and when certain Canadian personnel from the Canadian air force were transferred to the Royal Air Force. They served from, as far as I know, with the Royal Air Force for a considerable period and possibly until the end of the war. I cannot say how long they served, but in any event they served.
Some of these veterans became eligible for pensions. In the first instance they were required to go through exactly the same procedure as that which was required of Newfoundland veterans. In other words they were obliged to apply to the British ministry of pensions and try their luck there, and then

to come back to the Canadian pension commission for a supplement. Then after a while the government of Canada made a deal with the British ministry of pensions whereby the British ministry of pensions would pay a flat rate to the Canadian government and the Canadian government undertook to supplement it in order to bring it up to the Canadian level.
But I submit to the minister that it is mainly a matter of putting into effect the plain terms of the agreement between Newfoundland and Canada with respect to our veterans; and those terms are that, as far as Newfoundland veterans are concerned, having regard to their new applications, they will be treated as though they had served in Her Majesty's Canadian forces. That is all we are asking. I hope the minister will give consideration to this matter, and that when he replies he will set our minds and our hearts at rest with regard to whether anything is to be done about it at this session.
In theory the purpose of a resolution, as I understand it is to enable suggestions to be made prior to the bringing in of a bill so that all these wise suggestions can be incorporated in the legislation. I think that is something honoured more in the breach than in the observance. However, with respect to matters pertaining to veterans and veterans dependents, this is the only opportunity we shall have to do anything about it. Once we get the bill before us it will not be possible for us to bring in any amendment because then we shall be ruled out of order on the ground that any amendment we might propose in order to assist veterans will be a charge on the public treasury and, of course, under our rules it could not be permitted.
Therefore, before I sit down I want to make a few more suggestions which are going to cost the government a little bit of money, but which I hope the minister will see fit to incorporate in the amendment that he plans to set before us.
One big disappointment is that nothing has been said about extending benefits to the Newfoundland foresters of world war II. The president of the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit, Mr. Thomas Curran, and the secretary, Mr. C. R. Baggs, appeared before the standing committee on veterans affairs on March 31, 1960, and presented a brief which in my opinion was well and sympathetically received by the committee. In that brief they explained to the committee that they had performed exactly the same services as had been performed by the Newfoundland foresters of world war I. In world war II they had done exactly the same work as that done by the Canadian foresters, who often worked with them side by side; that they had taken
Pension Act
the same risks and undergone the same hardships, and that the only obstacle preventing them from receiving benefits is a technicality, namely that they were not put in uniform and organized as a battalion.
If we are interested in justice; if we want to do the right thing, surely we must realize that the right thing must be based on the merits of the case and not on technicalities such as whether a person had a uniform or whether he was recruited in a certain way. Certainly those technicalities should not be allowed to stand in the way of administering justice.
Then, of course, from time to time we have had requests from the merchant navy, from the rescue tug service and from the firefighters. All of them have very strong cases. If we are going to do justice to them we must base it on the merits of the service they perform and not on any technicality as to how they differ from the armed forces or things like that. These merchant navy people, the rescue tug service, performed services just as vital to the winning of the war as those performed by the other armed services, and in many cases the percentage of their casualties was higher.
Today in my own riding I have a number of crippled people who are incapable of earning a living and providing for their families because they contracted tuberculosis while cooped up in some freighter during the war, or because they were floating around in the ocean for 48 hours or 72 hours and contracted arthritis and all sorts of conditions and ailments arising out of the hardships which attended their service. Yet these people who served just as truly and just as nobly as did the others who were in the fighting forces are in this situation today, namely that they and their families must depend on public charity and public relief.
If Canada is ever going to find its soul, and if we are ever going to start to do the right thing, I do not think we should hedge about technicalities; rather we should do the thing that is right because it is right. I ask the minister if he will not try, even at this late date, to find some way of incorporating in his amendments measures which would do something for these people.
In closing I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Waterloo North with regard to continuing the pensions paid in respect of disabilities assessed at less than 50 per cent. In the case of the death of a veteran whose disability has been assessed at 50 per cent or more, the pension continues to be received by his widow and children; but in the case of a man who has suffered,

Pension Act
let us say, a degree of disability estimated at 45 per cent, the widow and family find their source of income cut off.
There seems to be injustice involved here, because if the principle is good in respect of 50 per cent it should be equally good in respect of 45 per cent or 35 per cent. We are not asking the government to extend the payment in respect of 50 per cent disability but to widen the principle so that those people concerned at least would not lose their source of income abruptly and be cast upon public relief and public charity.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
For many decades the members of the Progressive Conservative party have been the advocates of even better treatment for the veterans of our nation who served in the two world wars and also in other conflicts. While they sat on the opposition benches, the members of the Progressive Conservative party at all times asked that better pensions should be given to our veterans and that improved treatment should be accorded to those who had suffered from wounds resulting from their participation in action on the battlefield. They played a major part in securing from previous governments various improvements in the treatment of our veterans.
It is indeed gratifying to me to be an active member of a government which, ever since it secured power on June 10, 1957, has taken care of all those who served in those two wars and who, as a result of their devotion to duty were disabled on the battlefield. The former minister of veterans affairs, Hon. Mr. Brooks, devoted all his time and energies to improving the conditions existing in his department. He has, indeed, done a great job, and the veterans of this nation owe him a great many thanks and a debt of gratitude.
The work which he so ably performed is being carried on with efficiency and devotion by another veteran, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre the present holder of the portfolio of veterans affairs. As one who served during world war II, as a member of the War Amputations of Canada and of the Canadian Legion, I am pleased in the name of my fellow veterans to extend my thanks to the Minister of Veterans Affairs for the constant care which he shows for the disabled servicemen of this nation.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my colleagues of the War Amputations of Canada, and of all veterans of this country who, because they were wounded in various actions, must receive a government pension, I am very happy to

thank the former minister of veterans affairs, Senator Brooks, and the present minister (Mr. Churchill), for their magnificent work on behalf of our nation's veterans and their families.
Surely, among those who deserve the people's gratitude, none are more deserving than those who fought for months, and sometimes even for years, on the battlefields where our Canadian troops were called upon to serve and who, because of their devotion and heroism, now have to bear the scars of glorious wounds.
I want to pay a very particular tribute to those who laid down their lives because they wanted to serve their country and the cause of democracy. As I want to pay them a well-deserved tribute, I shall borrow the following verses from the poet Victor Hugo:
Ceux qui pieusement sont morts pour la patrle, Ont droit qu'a leur cercueil la foule vienne et prie, Entre les plus beaux noms, leur nom est le plus beau.
Toute gloire pres d'eux passe et tombe ephemere. Those who devotedly have died tor their country, Should rightly see the people flock to their graves to pray.
Among the greatest names theirs are the brightest. All glory, beside theirs, is fleeting ephemeral.
The heroic sacrifice of those who died at the front is equalled only by the sacrifice of those who, today, as victims of their duty, must still bear the pain of wounds received in action. For many of them, advancing years only add to their burden of suffering.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Weichel) mentioned that at the recent meeting of the War Amputations of Canada, 130 of our members who had died the previous year were missing at the roll call.
The veterans of the first great war are certainly due to disappear quite rapidly in the next few years, not only because the growing load of years affects them to a certain extent like everybody else, but also because, apart from that load, they have to bear that of their wounds which, in some cases, causes them to age before their time.
Several veterans of the second world war are now getting on in years. Some of them whom I know, find it impossible today to continue in their profession, which they had practised for many years, i.e. since the fighting ended in 1945.
Consequently, it is of capital importance to raise the level of veterans' pensions, and the action taken by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the goverment as a whole is certainly welcome at this time.

This increase will be a protection against the destitution which unfortunately, threatens quite a few of our veterans.
And while I am on the subject of the fate of veterans, I should like to pay a very special tribute to the personnel of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and particularly to those of hospitals caring for those of our veterans who, for some reason or other, have to be hospitalized.
When I came back from the war in 1945, I was fairly discouraged, and if it had not been for the good care and encouragement I received in veterans hospitals, I wonder whether my convalescence would have been as short, and if I could have made such rapid progress as I did.
This is perhaps the first opportunity I have in this house of addressing myself to the personnel of those hospitals, as well as to all those who serve in that department. And I am delighted to pay them the tribute due to them, and to thank them for all they are doing to help our war amputees and other veterans. It is from the bottom of my heart that, on behalf of all my comrades in arms, I express our most sincere appreciation for so many services rendered.
Before closing my remarks, I should also like to point out that our veterans are an example for the rest of our citizens. In fact, those men who, when the time came to serve their country on the battlefields, did so without hesitation, continue today in civil life to serve their country with dignity and competence. Only rarely will you meet a veteran who, today, does not occupy an important place in our national life; not very often, either, will you see a veteran who does not play some significant role in our country's economy.
Our veterans have learned to serve their country. They have understood the meaning of discipline. They have understood the necessity of obeying certain rules and, above all, they have learned the necessity of having esprit de corps and spirit of unity because, as everyone knows, to wage war individual effort is not enough; it requires the effort of a group which, united and fighting for the same cause and the same objective, strives to achieve the same goals. Our veterans continue to put into practice, in civil life, the spirit of co-operation which they have learned while serving their country.
I am proud to say that our veterans can rightly be considered as the best citizens of
Pension Act
this nation, because they have learned to understand the necessity of that unity while serving their country and fighting for the same cause and for the same objective. As a matter of fact, in their regiments never has race or religion separated one soldier from another; quite the contrary, regardless of their ethnic or racial origins, our soldiers fought hand in hand in splendid co-operation, realizing that it was in uniting themselves in battle, as they did, that they could achieve final victory, the ultimate objective, which was to save democracy as we understand it.
That national unity which our soldiers achieved in the service of their country, they still strive to strengthen through the efforts they make towards that end in their civil occupation.
I think the best example of that national unity can be found in such veterans' associations as the Canadian Legion, the Canadian War Amputations Association, the Paraplegic Society and other associations which maintain, in peacetime, that tradition of service and national unity for which so many of our people fought, for which so many suffered the consequences of glorious wounds or even made the supreme sacrifice.
I feel that the action taken by the government today constitutes an homage to those Canadians who fought in the army, the navy or the air force. For my part, I am proud to be a member of this government which gives such recognition to the services rendered by those veterans who have contributed to victory in two world wars and are now contributing to the establishment of peace.

I believe that the finest homage which can be rendered to these men may be found in these beautiful verses which we repeat at our reunions and which move us so deeply as we commemorate the memory of those who fell on the battlefields, victims of their duty and of their desire to serve their country. These verses-and I hope my memory shall not fail me-are as follows:
They shall grow not old. as we that are left grow old:
Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn. At the going down of the sun and in the morning We will remember them.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we all listened with a great deal ol interest and respect to the words of the Associate Minister of National Defence. We all appreciate his sincerity, integrity and emotion so calmly reflected in his remarks in view of his distinguished war record and his trials and tribulations as a result of his wounds suffered in the active service of our country. I was interested in the verse with which the hon. gentleman concluded his remarks. We fight a war on two fields in our lifetime, one on the battlefield and one at home. I wish to add to the words used by the hon. gentleman. In my opinion homage is best expressed in the words of Rudyard Kipling. They are these:
Not as a ladder from earth to heaven, not as a witness to any creed,
But simple service, simply given to his own kind in their common need.
To me that epitomizes humanity and citizenship in time of peace and war. That is the approach I wish to take in my brief remarks at this time.
I appreciated the associate minister's remarks. I can understand his taking advantage of this opportunity to pay homage to those who fought, those who died and those who returned in safety and their dependants who suffer because of the sacrifices in war. I cannot, however, agree with the remark of the minister that this has been foremost and uppermost in the devotion of the party which makes up the present government.
We in this group most certainly welcome resolution No. 9 on today's order paper which is now before us, for which the Minister of Veterans Affairs is asking the support of the house. He will most certainly receive the unanimous support of hon. members to bring in a bill to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependants, to permit payment of supplementary payments in certain cases, and to permit appeals from decisions in cases which are not now covered under the existing wording of the act which is subject to wrong decisions or misinterpretation.
But there is one thing I should like to draw to the attention of the Associate Minister of National Defence before he leaves the chamber. We welcome this resolution and what it purports to do. With respect to the statement as to the devotion of the Conservative party to the veterans, we wish the minister would have recalled that this legislation was supposed to come before the House of Commons last year. I say that because of the statement made in the veterans affairs committee of the year before to veterans organizations that appeared before the committee, that the legislation would be introduced in the House of Commons last year. Whatever

their devotion may be now, I am afraid they have been over a year late in fulfilling a promise given in the veterans affairs committee two years ago. I think this matter should be drawn to the attention of the Associate Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Read the committee report of two years ago and the statement of the minister. Recriminations are not important at the present time, but I had to draw this to the attention of he miniser.
We now have this resolution. I have received a great number of letters in regard to this matter, and this is why I rise in my place and speak at this time. Because of the language of the motion a number of us and many veterans are not quite certain as to how far it intends to go. It makes reference only to the Pension Act and to increases to disabled veterans and their dependants. The question I ask is, does this also cover changes in the veterans allowances? I refer to allowances to burnt out pensioners. My interpretation of this resolution is that it applies only to one act.

speechtext: That is right.

I thank the minister for nodding his head and saying that my interpretation is correct. Therefore I want to add my words to those of the veterans associations, and I am certain to those of many members of this House of Commons. It is absolutely correct that attention should be paid and is going to be paid to the disabled veterans and their dependants. Surely there should not be discrimination against those whose war services have been recognized in an act of parliament but who are not going to receive attention simultaneously with the ones who are covered in the resolution now before us and in the bill which will follow. It was because of recognition by parliament in the past of the effect of war on those who are not disabled, as they advance in years, that the veterans allowance act was brought into being. Their cost of living is the same as those who are disabled. For the life of me I cannot understand why, when by law these two groups of veterans are recognized for pension purposes, one group is left out when amendments are made to the Pension Act during this session of parliament.
There is not only this fact of discrimination now. They are already discriminated against because they have to face a means test. I think that should be revised upward right now. Even if no consideration is to be given to that surely the minister will give thought to those on war veterans allowance as well as those who are disabled. If there is a reason why there should be discrimination between these two groups of veterans,

perhaps the Minister of Veterans Affairs will have the courtesy and the kindness when he concludes this debate to tell us why the discrimination should be permitted to continue at this time. Why do those on veterans allowance not need an increase in the same way as those who are disabled?
May I also add my words to those of the hon. member for Waterloo North and ask the minister whether in this resolution he has given any thought or will give any thought to those in Canada and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, to those in his province in particular who went overseas in the forestry corps but do not receive benefits. Since the hon. member spoke of that matter in some detail I will not touch on it.
I am going to ask whether this resolution which deals with veterans gives any consideration to rectifying what I think is one of the most disgraceful things that has happened to those who went overseas and have never received any recognition. I refer to the recruiting of those who were asked to go overseas as firefighters. They were paid army pay but were never officially recognized in the same way as members of the active force on the battlefield itself, although they did serve under fire. According to statements I have received, they have never been recognized as eligible for veterans benefits and, I gather from the wording of the resolution, are not being recognized in the bill that is to be introduced following the passage of this resolution. I hope the new Minister of Veterans Affairs is giving some thought to those men who were under fire, who were recruited in Canada and did a necessary job overseas.
I said I was not going to speak at any length. There is only one other matter which I should like to place before the committee because it has been brought to my attention. I express the hope that the legislation to follow the resolution will give effect to the recommendation in the brief submitted to the Prime Minister and the cabinet by the Canadian Legion on December 12, 1960, with respect to a revised rate for dependant parents. If I may refer to that matter very briefly, on pages 7 and 8 of the brief the Legion points out that back in 1951 a widow received $75 and a dependant parent also received $75 whereas after the revision in 1951 the widow received $100 and the dependant parent $75. In addition, under the 1957 amendments the widow's rate was increased to $115 and the rate for a dependant parent to $90. As the Canadian Legion so aptly points out, there would seem to be no reason for this discrimination and the Legion recommends that the pension for a dependent
Pension Act
parent be restored to its former basis whereby the rate of payment was equal to that in the case of a widow with, of course, a more adequate additional amount where there are two dependant parents.
When the bill is before us and we know its details we will be able to discuss all aspects of this most important matter concerning our veterans with far more thoughtfulness and understanding. When the minister closes the debate I hope he will tell us about his approach to the financial problems of those on war veterans allowance. I hope he will also indicate whether anything is going to be done for those who fought overseas as foresters or firefighters. In particular, and of the utmost importance, I should like to know what the view of the Minister of Veterans Affairs is with regard to all aspects of the recommendations made by that most responsible organization, the Canadian Legion, on December 12, 1960.

speechtext:
I do not think that makes any difference. Maybe if he were a member of the committee he would understand things a lot more. I wanted to refer to the committee before saying anything about the resolution. As chairman of the committee last year I appreciate having worked with those who were members of the committee and also on former committees when I was a member though not the chairman.
I also want to say that I think we have received the greatest degree of co-operation from the officials of the department. Prior to my experience on the committee I did not have the slightest idea of the broad field of work that comes under veterans affairs, including hospitalization, the Veterans' Land Act, rehabilitation, etc. You will find very few veterans in this country who are not ready to stand up and say that they appreciate what has been done for them.
I do not propose to talk very long. The resolution has to do with amendments respecting disability pensions. It is true that it may not meet the wishes of all of us. I am not sure what the increases will be but I have a feeling that whatever they are they will be satisfactory to the great majority of disability pensioners in this country.
There are one or two points about which I wish to say something. One of them has been covered by my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo North. I have never been able to understand why a widow was denied a pension if her husband was not in receipt of at least a 50 per cent pension. I feel that the time has come when we should give consideration to wiping out that, what shall I call it, floor of 50 per cent. I believe that the widow should receive half of the pension the husband was receiving as long as she remains his widow. This has been my thinking for some time, and I am glad that the

matter has been mentioned. If we find the bill contains no provision in this respect, then we will keep on pressing for it and I am sure our representations will be given consideration.
There is another matter about which I wish to say a word or two, and about which the Canadian Legion has been rather critical. What I am about to say is not by way of criticism. Last year and the year before, if you look at the minutes of the standing committee, you will find there was considerable criticism of the Canadian pension commission's interpretation of section 70 of the act. This is known as the benefit of doubt section. We have been asked to make that section stronger. I should like to say to the minister, to other veterans and to the Canadian Legion, that I have studied this section and I do not see how parliament can do much more.
Every once in a while cases are brought before the committee which indicate that some veteran has not received the benefit of the doubt. Nevertheless I believe we should be very careful about passing judgment on this exercise of discretion by the Canadian pension commissioners until we have heard both sides of each case. I presume that the members of the Canadian Legion who have criticized these cases have heard both sides of the story. I feel that the deputy chairman of the Canadian pension commission outlined the situation very well, as I think anyone learned in the law will understand, when he said that the discretion left with a body or with an individual is exercisable by that body or individual. If the commission is not exercising its discretion to the satisfaction of those who appear before the committee there is not much parliament can do about it. We cannot appoint a man to a position and then tell him what to do.
I feel that over the years the governments have appointed men to the Canadian pension commission in whom they had confidence. On the whole I believe those members have done a fairly good job. It may be that they are overworked. It may be that we need to appoint more members to the commission. It may be that we need an appeal board set up within the pension commission itself.
Last year I noticed a reference to the fact that a claimant had to wait for several months in order to get his case reopened. The decision of the pension commission is final, but if an applicant can secure new evidence it is seldom, if ever, that the case cannot be reopened. This reopening of the case does not mean merely a review, but the case is tried from the beginning. It might save time if we had, as we have in the supreme courts of the provinces, an appeal

Pension Act
branch within the Canadian pension commission to which these cases could be referred. If after the final decision of the pension commission new evidence were procured the case could be taken directly to the appeal branch.
If I may return for a moment to the consideration of this question of discretion, I may say that I feel the pension commissioners have not been unfair. I suppose that if I were to take a number of cases to them and the commission turned them down I would feel they had not exercised their discretion properly under the benefit of doubt section. However, what may seem to me to be reasonable doubt might not seem to be a reasonable doubt to you, Mr. Chairman. This is our difficulty. I do not see how parliament can strengthen this provision because we have placed this discretion in the hands of the commissioners. The only thing we might do would be to impress upon the commissioners the fact that we feel they are not exercising their discretion in favour of the veteran. Perhaps if the commissioners felt we were not happy with the way they were exercising this discretion they would give these cases a second look, and they might take a more lenient view in the exercise of their discretion. I believe that an appeal board composed of men who had not heard these cases should be established so that these cases could be given further consideration.
In so far as veterans allowances are concerned, I have received few complaints in my area so I judge the people are happy about it. I just get the rare complaint. I do believe that at present the dependant parent of a deceased veteran, whose widow and children are receiving a pension can only get $40. I believe there is a point there to which we could give consideration. I do not believe $40 is sufficient. However, I will not go as far as some other hon. members. After all, this dependant's allowance is like the war veterans allowance and was given in lieu of the old age pension. If a married couple are both receiving the old age pension they can get $115. There are many points to be considered in this argument. I believe that governments, over the years, have been gradually more generous. I believe these cases must be considered from every standpoint. I do not like to see a member get up in the house and commence to rail about these poor people.
The veterans, especially the disability pensioner who was wounded on the battlefield, are not asking for sympathy. The pensions we are giving them for the loss of arms or legs or something like that are not sufficient to repay them for these losses, but these same pensioners will tell you that they would rather see the boys who did not get
any recognition receive some pension than to get an increase in their pensions. These veterans who saw service are amongst the most generous citizens in this country.
I do not think I will take up any more of the time of the committee. Whatever increases are provided in this bill, they will be appreciated. No doubt there are other things to be tidied up. I have no doubt that our present minister is working on that matter with his officials.
There is another point that should be given consideration but it cannot really be raised or should not be raised on this resolution. I refer to the situation of a veteran who may be getting the veterans' allowance and the pension. He may not get the benefit from this legislation unless there is an amendment to another act. However, these things can not be handled together. Each must be considered on its own merits. I have all the faith in the world in our present Minister of Veterans Affairs. I am confident that these points we are raising will not be overlooked. Whether or not they can be dealt with at this session, I believe it is a good thing to mention them and I believe that they will receive consideration.

This bill seems to me to personify some of the faults which are inherent in our present system, particularly in relation to primary industry. What is the Aurora Pipe Line Company? One-third of the shares are held by the Hudson's Bay Company, and two thirds of those shares are held by the Continental Oil Company which is a large United States oil enterprise. because of the fact that it owns Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, and because the executive officers of the Aurora Company are executive officers of the Hudson's Bay Company, is a subsidiary of one of the largest oil companies operating either in Canada or the United States.
It has been said that this bill would be referred to two or three governing bodies charged in Canada with the regulations of gas, oil and energy. speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to make a speech we will be happy to hear it when the time arrives for him to stand up and reply. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. If the hon. member will permit me to interrupt, I have very grave doubts about the relevancy of this debate in the line which it has taken. It is true that this bill is to incorporate a private company with power to transport oil, gas and other liquid hydrocarbons but only subject to the provisions of any general legislation relating to pipe lines for the transmission and transportation of gas, so that if the house passes the bill which only gives the company a power or capacity-it does not put it in the oil or gas business-in view of the other legislation which controls companies formed for the transportation of petroleum products in Canada I would think that with such a limited purpose or effect as there is in a bill of this kind, the house would be going beyond any reasonable discussion of such a bill if it discussed the industrial situation in the country even in the context of petroleum products.
It would, of course, be relevant to say that there are enough companies in this field and we should not create even another company with the powers that this bill would give, but my point is-and I think the point is important enough to raise it-that on every
Private Bills
bill to incorporate a private company we would not want to open a full scale debate on the industry or the economy of the country in the field in which that company intended to operate. I do not believe the house would expect to follow that course.
I do not accuse the hon. member who has the floor of initiating this irrelevant debate which began the last time this bill was before the house but I do say that the bill relates to the desirability of giving to another private company the corporate powers to enter into the petroleum pipe line field rather than to the economics of that field into which it proposes to enter. I say this because the bill only gives a corporate power and does not put the company in business. It can only enter into the business, as the bill itself says:
-subject to-the provisions of-any-general legislation relating to pipe lines enacted by parliament with respect to the transmission and transportation of oil and other liquid hydrocarbons-
Parliament must take notice of the licensing legislation which it has already passed.

I know we all fully understand the point you have raised but may I, sir, with all respect point out that although the bill itself speaks of incorporating a company, the act would be completely meaningless unless after incorporation the company could export. Therefore, in deciding on the fundamental principle of the House of Commons and the Senate granting an act of incorporation it is obvious that after the bill goes through all the various stages before the company can carry out its function it has to export hydrocarbons, methanes, butanes and condensates of the production of the gas field. The bill is meaningless unless the company can export. Surely the principle that we should discuss is the end result after the company goes through all its procedures and gets incorporation.

If you desire more on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something. I feel that the question of the export of hydrocarbons is a matter of policy which has been settled by legislation of this parliament. It has been determined that it can be done provided that certain conditions are met, and those conditions have been embodied in legislation, namely the national energy board legislation. Whether or not that is wise legislation is not open for discussion on this bill. This bill merely asks the house to decide whether certain persons interested should have the corporate capacity and be created a corporation for the purpose of then exporting, if they meet the law. The law as to whether or not they are entitled to export is determined by other legislation that has already

Private Bills
been passed. With great deference I submit it is not open, however much we may desire to do so, to argue now whether that was a right policy or a wrong policy. It is only open to us to argue on the suitability of those applicants to have corporate capacity.
For that purpose.

Corporate capacity for the purpose, but the policy is not open to be argued at all, because that has been settled and is governed by other legislation which is not before the house on second reading of this bill.
I did not want to interrupt the hon. member, but I think the debate-and I am not saying this in criticism of the hon. members -has been ranging away beyond the area that is permissible in the particular bill before the house at this time. Many of the matters that have been argued are matters of broad general policy which have no application to the bill before us to incorporate a private company.

On the point of order, especially in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West who has just spoken, it seems to me that if we follow the suggested course of action we would be going completely contrary to the rules of the house, as I understand them as they apply to private bills. These rules have been in existence for quite a few years since I have been here and in many years before that. If we follow that reasoning, Mr. Speaker, it would lead us purely and simply to consider the company itself without any consideration as to its relationship with the economy and the industry within which it will function, or anything of that nature.
I do not think we should attempt now to reverse the precedents that have been followed in this house for many years. In the past we have given consideration to the effect of a particular bill upon the industry within which a company would be functioning after it became incorporated. In this case, we should give consideration to the industry within which this company will function after it is incorporated and passes the other obstacles of the national energy board, and so on.
It was not the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), as you yourself mentioned, who initiated this type of discussion; it was the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith). The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) moved the motion on behalf of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams). The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), along with the hon. member for Winnipeg South, initiated the discussion of the relationship of this

company, after incorporation, with another company already incorporated, or two other companies, and with the industry itself, in an attempt to determine whether it is advisable or not at this time to give endorsation to the incorporation of this particular company. I think we must be allowed to follow that general relationship between the company we are now considering and others and especially its relationship to the industry and to other companies; otherwise, we shall just be blindly endorsing every application that comes before parliament without considering the effect it will have upon other sectors of the economy, including instances of incorporation by acts of this parliament itself.
With deference and respect, sir, I suggest that in this instance the debate should be allowed to continue on the same basis as have similar debates in the past and that we should be permitted to take into account the effect of this incorporation upon other parts of the same industry and upon our economy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I want to thank hon. members who have assisted me with the problem which I raised myself as a point of order. I think it is clear, and hon. members will agree, that what we are debating is the principle of the bill before us on second reading, not the details. As I see it, the principle of the bill is whether this group of individuals petitioning parliament shall be given corporate capacity. I see no principle other than this involved in this bill, whether this particular group of individuals shall be given corporate capacity.
Now, from the giving of that corporate capacity under this bill when it is passed other consequences may flow. That is true; but whether they will flow or not is purely conjectural. This bill could be passed and nothing might follow. If anything follows it will be in accordance with licensing legislation which has been passed by this house in which this house has already declared its policy. For this reason I think the debate has gone beyond reasonable bounds in discussion of the principle which is really at stake, namely whether this group shall have corporate powers.
I can see the difficulty which arises because the hon. member who sponsored the bill went on to expound what the company's intention would be after it had been incorporated, and that put in issue some of the things that the hon. member is talking about. Therefore, I am not disposed at this point to say that there shall be no discussion of the probable effects of the activity of this company in the context of the oil transport industry; but I do say that ordinarily it is not a necessary part of the discussion of such a

principle except to say that there are enough companies in the field, and this particular company should not be incorporated. I hope I will not do any injustice to any member in asking that the discussion be restricted to the plans of this company as declared in the debate and not to a general debate on the economies of the oil industry.
