Mr. Speaker, I am in particular agreement with one thing you said, namely that if this bill passes and nothing else comes of it we shall have a pipe line coming from some place and going nowhere for no particular reason. I do not want to question the argument because I think it is a sound one. However, I should like to read a part of the statement made by the sponsor of the bill in the other place. He referred to a press release that appeared in a number of newspapers, which release was in these words:
Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited has filed an application with the Alberta government seeking permission to construct a 41 mile pipe line for transportation of unrefined condensate from gas fields in southwestern Alberta to the international border.
The company's proposed line would cost an estimated $1,700,000. It would consist of 11 miles of 4 inch pipe from the Waterton-Castle river area to the Fincher creek field and 30 miles of 8 inch pipe from the Pincher Creek field to the international border near Carway. Maximum capacity of the line would be 32,600 barrels daily, and early movement would range from 4,000 to 8,000 barrels daily.
The pipe line would connect at the border with a pipe line system being constructed by Continental Pipe Line Company, the wholly owned subsidiary of Continental Oil Company. Continental Pipe Line is constructing a pipe line from Cut Bank, Montana, via Billings to Platte Pipe Line Company's Byron station near Powell, Wyoming. It is planned to extend this system from Cut Bank to the international border to connect with the proposed Hudson's Bay system.
It is indicated here, Mr. Speaker, that this line will serve no Canadian purpose at all, that its only purpose is to connect two existing gas fields in Canada with a United States distribution system already in existence not far from the border and from which a line is already being extended to a point on the international border. I believe this raises immediately the question of whether this line should exist at all. I am of the opinion that it should not exist at this time or at any time until we have explored all the possibilities of establishing in what appears to be a new field in Canada the handling and processing of these condensates from the washing of the natural gas industry.
I have been told that if we were to establish in Canada an industry which would handle these condensates we would have a number of secondary industries established for the initial processing of the by-products, and this might then warrant eventually a 90205-6-115

line from these secondary industries to handle those by-products which could not be used in Canada. We might then find it in our interests to export to the Continental Oil Company of the United States. We might find it advantageous at that time to construct a line then solely for the purpose of joining our producing areas to the United States market through their distribution systems.
I believe that if we build this line at the present time we will be defeating ourselves and doing away with the opportunity to establish secondary indusmes in that field to use the by-products which would be available locally and which would have to be processed in that area if this export transmission line is not constructed. Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise to a point of order, at the risk of spending a good deal of time on points of order. I would refer Your Honour, first, to citations 482 and 483 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition. I shall read what I believe are the relevant parts of these citations, but I give the reference to them in case anyone wants to pursue the matter.
Does this have to do with what I was saying?

It has to do with that very point. This citation refers to the second reading of a bill as follows:
There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.
Citation 483 reads as follows:
The house does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill, the house is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it is afterwards referred finds those allegations proved.

Then it goes on to say that it is usual, therefore, to allow a second reading, except when the bill enunciates some principle which the house is not prepared to affirm. My point is that the hon. member is seeking to allege here certain facts in connection with the persons seeking incorporation and also certain other facts which are in doubt concerning other pipe line companies. These matters of fact can be dealt with properly only in the committee. They are not matters that can be inquired into on the second reading of a private bill in the house because there is no machinery for dealing with them, and with the whole matter that is now before us. Whether we should agree to the proposed incorporation would be a matter of fact to be determined in the committee and, therefore, for these reasons I respectfully submit the hon. member is going beyond what is permissible at this stage.

I would only comment on that by saying that the practice of the house itself, since I have been here, has misled me. It has been completely inconsistent with what the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mc-Ilraith) has said. If the citation to which the hon. gentleman has referred is correct-I can only say it has been the practice on each occasion to go into these questions if an hon. member desired to participate in such a debate on a private bill-and if that is the rule the house desires to follow, I think perhaps it would be unkind and unfair to some members, especially in view of what other hon. members have said before this matter was raised.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I accept the authorities which have been cited from Beauchesne's fourth edition. I think it is a sound statement of principle. I also recognize that the practice in debating private bills has often allowed a wide-ranging debate without objection from the house. That fact, of course, does not alter the principle. The fact that the house goes beyond what is a proper debating course without objection being taken does not establish a new rule. That result would not follow unless exception is taken and the point is raised and dealt with. I therefore think that the hon. member should not rely too heavily on debates in which he has taken part or which have occurred in the past.
I have been looking at the previous discussions of this matter in order to see how far the sponsors have opened the facts as expressed by the people who are applying for incorporation. It was because of that initial discussion that I did not feel I could properly stop comment on what had been raised earlier in the debate on behalf of the sponsors. I still feel that way about the matter, although

I recognize the fact that the discussion has largely been ranging beyond proper debate on a private bill the principle of which is quite limited in that it only give corporate capacity and does not do any of the things which hon. members have been discussing.

From what you have said, Mr. Speaker, I gather that it is all right to stretch the rule a little bit as long as you are not caught or as long as no one objects to your doing so. The last time this subject was debated hon. members of that group-
Meaning us.
-indicated that they wanted more information on the subject, that they needed certain particulars dealing with the export of the product concerned, yet today they moved to close the debate so that it could not be re-opened in this house.

speechtext: Would the hon. member give me that page reference again?

Do not put words in my mouth.

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Hamilton (York West) in the chair:
That, it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependants; to permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I interrupted my remarks at five o'clock, pursuant to the rule which says that private bills must be discussed between five and six o'clock, I had just referred to some remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria-Car-leton (Mr. Montgomery), and I was trying to relate his words to a statement the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) made on December 12, 1980.
In that statement that at five o'clock I qualified as quite broad and which I could now call omnibus, I understood-I hope I was right-that there was some possibility that an amendment could be made to section
Pension Act
70 of the act. This section deals with the benefit of the doubt to be granted to veterans who claim a pension and I would like to put the text on record. Section 70 reads as follows:
(Text):
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, on any application for pension the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
(Translation):
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton told us a while ago-and I hope I did not mis-contrue his words-that it was almost impossible to improve the wording in order for the commission or "the body adjudicating on the claim" to be in a position, because of a new wording, to make better decisions. It is evident that veterans-because in most cases claims are examined by veterans-use their discretion, as they are allowed to do under the law. But there are some cases where we, who had to deal with similar cases, feel that they do not exercise discretion as they should.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said that in his opinion it was impossible to improve the act. It is my humble opinion that it is always possible to improve an act and the Minister of Veterans Affairs should, with the help of his officials-if he has not already done so-undertake a special study of section 70 in the light of the cases which were submitted to the Canadian pension commission, and try at least to find a new formula or rewrite the law so that veterans be given full justice.
Mr. Chairman, I think of at least two cases at this time. The first is the case of a veteran of the 1914-18 war, who fought in the trenches with the formation now called the Royal 22nd Regiment and who, after spending days and nights and whole weeks in insanitary trenches, as they all were, is now suffering from rheumatism and other malformations but does not receive any pension. Why? Because the physicians who testified before the pension commission of the time could not state whether the rheumatism from which he was suffering at that time and from which he is still suffering today was really due to his war service hardships. Well, in my humble opinion, it is normal to assume that the disease which then affected him and still continues now was due to his war service. And yet

Pension Act
he could not get any pension. That is a case where, I think the party in question should have been given the benefit of the doubt.
I am thinking also of another case which comes under subsection 2 of section 13 of the act since it has to do with peace time service. That young man who is now dead was suffering from a disease whose origin is now the physicians could not establish. Well the physicians cannot state whether the disease has resulted from his peacetime service or from other causes.
Well, if doctors cannot say that the illness is due to some other causes, I believe the widow of this young man should have received benefits, if he was otherwise entitled to a pension. This case is still pending and I hope that following my remarks, the minister or his officials will decide to bring in a new formula regarding section 70 of the act, so that dependents of deceased veterans might receive the benefits they are entitled to.
Mr. Chairman, our Criminal Code, relying on the theory of the benefit of the doubt, states that the accused is considered innocent until proven guilty. I believe the same should apply in the case of the benefits to be paid to veterans as well as to those who devote their energy and their health to the service of our country, both in time of peace and of war. Really, they should get the benefit of the doubt when it comes to finding the cause of the diseases they could have caught during their service either in time of peace or war.
Those are the main remarks I wanted to make on this matter. I am convinced that the Minister of Veterans Affairs, himself a veteran, will give them kind consideration. There is no doubt that our veterans, those young men who made the sacrifice of their life or their health for the defence of their country, are entitled to our consideration. There should be no party politics involved in this house or in the veterans affairs committee on this matter. We all want to cooperate for the welfare of our veterans.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because of the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East I feel that I should place on the record at this time a part of the statement made by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs when he referred in this house to the record of accomplishment of this government under the previous minister as reported at page 734 of Hansard of December 12, 1960:
During Colonel Brooks' term of office $471 million was added by the consent of parliament to the

amounts already being received by our veterans in disability pensions, war veterans allowances, increases to widows and dependent parents, educational assistance to children, and increases for hospitals. Under Colonel Brooks' guidance the house increased the basic rates for war veterans allowances and raised the ceilings for permissible earnings. Residence requirements for allied vet-terans were lowered from 20 to 10 years; veterans with a year's service in the United Kingdom became eligible for allowances; that is, veterans of world war I. Equity in recipients' homes was raised; allowances may now be paid to veterans living abroad who had 12 months' prior residence in Canada; loans under the Veterans' Land Act were increased, as well as home construction loans.
The minister went on to point out:
From world war I there are now approximately
240.000	survivors. Of that number approximately
49.000	are pensioners; slightly over 25 per cent of the total number of survivors of the first world war. The veteran survivors of the second world war number 826,000, and of that number somewhat over 100,000, or slightly over 12 per cent, are pensioners.
At the present time some 5,000 children of world war I pensioners and over 160,000 children of world war II pensioners are receiving assistance.
In the standing committee on veterans affairs set up by this government I have heard it said by delegations who have appeared before us that this government has done more for veterans in the three years it has been in power than had been accomplished in any previous period of time. That is not to say that some of the points raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East should not concern us at this time just as much as they concern him.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, the chairman of the standing committee, we are concerned about the benefit of the doubt section. Let me quote briefly from a statement contained at page 10 of the brief of the Canadian Legion presented to the government on December 12, 1960:
Nearly 50 per cent of cases heard at appeal in the fiscal year 1958-59 were successful.
It is inconceivable that of the number of cases turned down after the first hearing half of them should have been allowed on appeal. It seems to me the benefit of the doubt is not being given to applicants. I support what the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton says to the effect that it is difficult to express in words what a commission shall do. You must pick good men and leave it up to them. Perhaps their hands may be tied in certain ways.
An amendment should be introduced to this section and according to the statement

of the minister something is going to be done in this respect. Speaking in this house on December 12, 1960 as reported at page 736 of Hansard, the minister said:
In some instances, the act and the interpretation of the act have limited the activities of the pension commission, and in the revision that is now going on it is our hope that some of the sections which have hindered the commission from time to time may be altered so that its work may become more effective.
Each of us will have to place his own interpretation on the words contained in that paragraph. We will not know what will be accomplished until the bill comes before us. I trust that some improvement will be brought about with respect to section 70. I also wish to refer to a statement in the Canadian Legion brief respecting conditions not recorded on enlistment:
The Legion has on record cases in which the pension commission has pointed to the lack of record of a disability on discharge and has ruled that in view of this it must be accepted that in fact there was no disability present at this time. Why then should not the commission be bound by enlistment examinations? The commission rules a condition to be of a pre-enlistment nature and then draws a totally unwarranted conclusion that there was no aggravation during service in many cases where there is a disability recorded on discharge and none on enlistment.
This problem and this section of the act are linked together with the benefit of the doubt section.
We have heard a lot about the firefighters and foresters. The hon. member for Vancouver East was most eloquent in speaking of this group of people who went overseas and performed a very worth-while function but in my opinion the forgotten people in terms of our veterans legislation are the merchant seamen. Coming from a coastal city I am keenly interested in this group. Knowing that the merchant navy suffered over 25 per cent casualties and that the provisions in the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act are very limited in scope it seems to me our merchant seamen deserve better treatment. I sincerely hope that the merchant seamen who have appeared year after year before the veterans affairs committee will somehow or other be brought under the provisions of those acts which now apply solely to veterans.
There are other problems which are of a technical nature and which could be corrected at very little expense. I know that recently in Vancouver the minister spoke to a meeting of some 400 legionnaires representing, I would guess some 15 branches, during the afternoon. I know he also had different meetings with officials from various Legion
Pension Act
branches who came up and discussed their problems with him. I know the minister was most sympathetic to them and will try to do what he can to bring about at least some of the changes which have been requested.
I might mention that some of these changes have to do with the regulations which limit the equity that a widow may have under the War Veterans Allowance Act on the death of her husband. I realize that this is not under discussion at the present time but it is bound up in this whole matter of veterans pensions. For instance, I know a person who was told she was $500 over the amount allowed. Her husband was a recipient of war veterans allowance. He died and as a single person she has too much money to the extent of $500 to qualify. When you consider that $2,000 is the top limit allowed you can see that it is not too much to take care of those extraordinary costs which are incurred at a time of sickness or to make major repairs to a house, and so on. But she has to get rid of this amount, and it seems to me to be a rather stupid bureaucratic regulation. It could be changed without amendment to the act.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer. Last year this government permitted pensions to be paid to veterans outside of Canada; but under the regulations, after having qualified to receive a pension outside of Canada, if the veteran dies his widow and children, if there are children, must return to Canada and live in this country a year before they can go back to wherever they had established themselves. This seems rather ridiculous to me. It is something that should never have been put in the regulations and it should be changed.
I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee but I do believe that this government has more veterans than any previous government had, both backbenchers and members of the cabinet. This government set up the standing committee on veterans affairs. At least 90 per cent of the members of that committee are veterans. I do not say this is a good thing. I am one who believes that there should be a larger number of nonveterans on this committee. Some hon. members may think that if we had a committee dealing with medicine we should have only doctors on that committee. There is no reason why all the members of this committee should be veterans. The committee should have representatives from all sides of the house, regardless of whether they are veterans or not.
This committee has done a good job and this government has done a good job in regard to veterans legislation. We must never forget

Pension Act
the debt we owe to the veterans of world wars I and II. It is something that we can never repay, but the requirements of this group of citizens must not only be considered in relation to the requirements of all other groups, but also taking into due account the tremendous service they have given to this country and what we owe these men and women. However, we still must legislate with justice to all. I believe this government has done this.
Generally speaking, we may say that veterans legislation is something on which we do not draw party lines. All members of the veterans affairs committee speak, not as members of different parties but as parliamentarians with the best interest of veterans at heart. But if veterans legislation is to be thrown into the political field then this government and this party can stand on their own feet and show a record that is second to none. This party can show that it has done more for veterans than any other party has ever done; this party can show that it has carried the torch, that we have kept faith. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it would be very ill advised on the part of the opposition parties to challenge us on this phase of our program.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who spoke for all the Newfoundland members on this side of the house. I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment and to thank him and his predecessor in the department for the courtesy and promptness with which they have dealt with the problems I have had occasion to send to them from time to time. The importance of the resolution before the committee is, I am sure, appreciated by all hon. members. The debt owed by the nation to its veterans is, I feel quite sure, completely understood and I will not presume to comment further on it or enlarge on this theme.
Beneficial measures designed to help the veterans must, of course, have our approbation. However, I feel that I should mention the forestry unit from Newfoundland which served overseas during world war II. Their desire is to be given the same treatment as is accorded to members of the Canadian forestry corps.
It has been pointed out by members of the forestry unit that they did not wear His Majesty's uniform but they did work side by side with the Canadian forestry corps, and many of them did serve in the home guard in the British Isles. I know that some of those men today are ill and in need, and the only assistance they can get is from welfare
[Mr. Broomed
sources. I do not think these men should be the recipients of charity and I hope that provision can be made to bring the members of the Newfoundland forestry unit under the act and that arrangements can be made to have them participate in veterans benefits.
I should also like to ask for consideration for the merchant marine, the rescue tug service and the fire fighters. The reference made to the status of Newfoundland servicemen by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo is one which really deserves immediate attention. Under the law, Newfoundlanders became Canadians when Newfoundland entered confederation. Not only that, but it was clearly specified that their status was to be as if they had been always Canadians. For instance, if a Newfoundlander were asked to state the country of his birth he would have to say Canada although he was born in Newfoundland before confederation. Although we entered confederation in 1949 we have always been Canadians. That is the law. It does seem strange, therefore, that there is still a difference in the status of Newfoundland veterans vis-a-vis Canadian veterans. It just is not consistent. It is wrong and it is a wrong that should be righted.
There is another point I should like to mention. In marginal cases when decisions are being made as to whether the veteran deserves to receive benefits, the benefit of the doubt seldom is given to the veteran. At least it seems so to me. I think this is also wrong. The very spirit of the administration of veterans affairs should be to give the benefit of the doubt to the veteran. Imponderables which it is impossible to pin down as facts are often associated with veterans requests. In such circumstances, rather than risk an unjust decision which can leave a veteran in need or without medical aid it seems to me that it is the fair thing and the wise thing to "let mercy season justice".

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak very briefly on the resolution. I realize there are many other hon. members who wish to speak and none of us wishes to delay the implementation of this legislation. Because this is the first opportunity I have had to do so, I should like to compliment the Minister of Veterans Affairs on the assumption of his portfolio. His service in the two world wars of this century, in the first one as a very young man and in the last as the commanding officer of a fine regiment, and his deep understanding of the problems of his fellow Canadians have fitted him for this most important of portfolios and we wish him every success.
I should also like to compliment the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans

Pension Act
Affairs upon his appointment. Those of us who have worked with the hon. member for Saskatoon in recent years realize how fair-minded, industrious and conscientious he is and I personally wish him well as I am sure we all do.
It has been said that Canada's veterans' legislation is second to none in the world but then that is only as it should be. Though I may perhaps be disagreeing slightly with one hon. member on my own side of the house, it seems to me that our veterans legislation is a tribute to all those in all parties who have served in previous parliaments because over the years members of all parties have tried to make our veterans legislation the best that it possibly could be, and that is as it should be.
In the last 62 years Canadians have gone forth four times from this country to fight our wars, the Boer war, the two great wars and Korea. Their service and sacrifice have done more than anything else, it seems to me, to raise us to the honoured place that we hold in the world today, and we do hold an honoured place. We owe a great debt to our veterans and to the dependants of our veterans, one which in many cases money can never repay.
I can well remember half a dozen or more years ago attending a Remembrance Day service at the national war memorial here in Ottawa. That year a change was made in the service from what it had been in the years before. A mother was asked to come on November 11 and place a wreath at the memorial on behalf of those mothers who had lost sons in Canada's wars. I believe the idea was that of the Very Reverend Dean Anderson, at that particular time dominion president of the Canadian Legion. I should like to give credit to him for it if indeed it was his idea. On this particular day a mother from Saskatchewan who had lost three sons in world war II, two boys in the air force and one in the army, took part in the service. As she stood there after placing her wreath I do not think there was a dry eye among the thousands who were watching. There is not enough money in the world to pay that mother or any other mother for the lads they gave to fight for this country.
The last revision of the Pension Act was in 1957, a welcome and generous revision, but I feel it is time that the act should be revised again, as is it being done. Civil service salaries have been raised and the pay of the armed forces has been increased. I believe and I am sure we all believe that this measure to increase veterans pensions and the pensions of dependents will be welcomed everywhere. It seems to me that the 90205-6-116
editorial pages of our newspapers mirror the thoughts of Canadians. The front pages are set up mainly to sell newspapers but the editorial pages usually tell us the truth. I should like to refer to an editorial in the Fredericton Gleaner of December 14, 1960, headed "Disabled War Veterans", which reads as follows:
It there is one thing Canada can afford to do it is to reimburse her disabled war veterans for the hell they endured in the two global wars of this century. Debate has started in the commons on government legislation to boost their pensions. We hope it will not be prolonged, that the measure will be passed into law without delay.
Canada's war veterans are entitled to a decent standard of living. They gave their arms, their legs, their eyes and suffered fearful wounds when duty called them to the colours. Now, in many cases, they are unable to earn their livelihood as whole men can. Canada should not hesitate in doing her duty to them.
A moment's reflection is all it takes to realize that, were it not for these valiant soldiers, sailors and airmen, Canadians might not have the privilege of debating their country's problems at all.
One criticism we sometimes hear is that some veterans is getting a pension and does not deserve one. Perhaps that is true. Those of us who were in the services know that there were always fellows around who did not seem to be very much good. They were no good before they went into the services and they were no good as soldiers, sailors or airmen. Having worked with some of them after the war in the Legion and later as a member of this house it is apparent that they are no good now either. Perhaps some of them are getting pensions. That is possibly true. It has always been the policy of the pension commission and the war veterans allowance board over the years to lean over backwards in awarding pensions so that some deserving man will not be left out.
We hear a great deal of criticism about the "benefit of the doubt." My own personal feeling is that if there is any doubt at all the veteran does get the benefit of the doubt. I feel that Mr. Anderson and the pension commission and Colonel Cromb and the war veterans allowance board are bending over backwards to give the veteran a fair break every time.
When we read the Legionary we often see pictures with a caption saying why disability pensions are paid. I should like to tell hon. members very briefly about a case before I finish. It concerns a member of this house. He led his company of the North Nova Scotia Highlanders on D-day across the beaches of Normandy and then through some of the terrible battles that followed. Finally one day in the fields of Normandy a shell landed and shrapnel shattered his arm. His arm was hanging by a piece of muscle and he could not leave it like that. He asked his batman

Pension Act
who was near him to cut it off for him but the man could not. I can see why he could not. So this officer had his batman open his clasp knife and he performed his own amputation above the elbow. Even after that he continued to lead his company in action until he finally collapsed from pain and loss of blood. He lay there for most of the day until he became unconscious. After being found he regained consciousness three days later having been given constant transfusions of blood and plasma. He is one of those who does not feel that this country owes him a living. By the way, I am speaking of the hon. member for Colchester-Hants. I think he is an example to all Canadians. He does not feel that this country owes him a living.
He has said more than once that all any veteran's pension should do is to compensate him for what he has lost. It is not intended to keep him completely, but it is intended to compensate him for what he has lost. I know that the people, not only in my own constituency but in the whole of Canada, will urge our very able Minister of Veterans Affairs and our very able government to be as generous as possible to the veterans and the veterans dependants of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this item I should like first to commend the Minister of Veterans Affairs for bringing this resolution before this committee. I should like also to congratulate him on his new appointment as minister of this department. I am certain that with his wise counsel and with his service record, the department will benefit from his leadership and his experience. At this time also I should like to take the opportunity to express the gratitude of the people I represent, the veterans of Swift Current-Maple Creek, to the previous minister, now a senator, for the concern, sympathy and understanding which he gave to the many veterans' problems with which he dealt during the time he held this portfolio. It was during his tenure of office that the standing committee on veterans affairs was established. I am sure those of us who have served on that committee, regardless of party affiliation, will agree that it was to a large extent as a result of his interest in the welfare of veterans that Canada's veterans legislation is considered to be the finest anywhere in the world, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury said.
This does not alter the fact, however, that this legislation must be kept up to date and adjustments made in it from time to time. The resolution before us is the forerunner of the bill to amend the Pension Act, and actually it is broken down into four distinct clauses. The first clause would provide for increased pensions to disabled veterans and their dependants; the second would permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; the third would permit appeals 90205-6-116i
Pension Act
from decisions of the former board of pensions commissioners; and the fourth would provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.
I trust that the measures to implement the first two clauses of this resolution will cover the ninth recommendation contained in the 1959 brief of the Canadian Legion wherein they recommend that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war who is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment will be entitled to have such injury or disease presumed to have had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
I believe that recommendation deserves serious consideration by the minister and by his officials. As we all now know, and has been mentioned previously this evening, Mr. Anderson, who is now chairman of the pension commission, was a former official of the Canadian Legion. I hope that he uses his high office in order to influence the minister and the rest of the staff to implement this resolution.
In the time allotted to me I propose to deal mainly with the last two clauses of this resolution which are as follows:
-to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Many of us who are members of some service organization such as the Canadian Legion have had some experience in establishing claims for pension on behalf of our comrades. My recollection is that the more conscientious the individual was during his term of service, the more difficult it was to establish his claim for pension. I do not blame any board or any officials of the department for this difficulty because they have no alternative but to follow the act and the regulations concerning that matter. I could say a great deal about the regulations with regard to any of these acts. I am quite sure that when the act was passed, if the regulations were then before the house, many of these regulations would have been changed because to my mind in many cases the regulations are more powerful than is the act itself.
Many of us know of cases of service personnel who would have to be flat on their back before they would report to their medical officers. As a result no record appears on their documents of any minor ailment they may have had because the doctors themselves did not report to their medical officer. In later years when these service personnel were back in civil life those ailments, through aggravation or other causes, forced them to seek

Pension Act
medical attention. In obtaining medical histories of their patients the civilian doctors concluded that the source of aggravation was traced back to war services. In very few cases from my experience with the board of pension commissioners do they accept the civilian doctor's findings, stating there was no entry on the applicants' service records. The term N.A.D.-no apparent disability- used on discharge from a hospital oftentimes if the truth were known revealed the lack of experience of some doctors in diagnosing the case.
In trying to establish proof of claim at this late date the pension commission has requested veterans to contact their service medical officer who treated them during their term of service. If the treatment was minor and the patient was not a malingerer the medical officer could not be expected to recall any particular patient being treated 15 years or 20 years ago for a minor unrecorded ailment.
With the amendment to permit further appeal from decisions of the board of pension commissioners I am certain that many deserving cases should and will be reviewed, claim will be established and entitlement granted. Many service organizations and members of parliament here in this House of Commons today who have spoken on this resolution obviously feel that the .pension commission have failed to extend the provisions of section 70 of the Canadian Pension Act, commonly known or referred to as the benefit of the doubt clause to applicants for pension. There appears to be ample evidence, as some of the members who have been on this committee have stated, filed with the department that the commission did not use this section in the manner in which many of us believe it was intended to be used.
Before we get off on the wrong track about what this benefit of doubt means may I say this. I have heard some statements here in the house today which do not apply to this section. The benefit of the doubt refers only to the medical records of the service personnel. We are not doubtful about whether the board has done the right thing or about whether they have leaned over backwards. The benefit of the doubt refers to the medical records.
I have always been an advocate of the principle that those who volunteer for service and were disabled by any means while in the service should be eligible for pension. I say that volunteers should be shown the respect that is due to them. It was no fault of theirs that they were not called for service in a theatre of war. They volunteered to go where the Canadian government wanted them to go. As I have said, the very fact

that they volunteered seems to have been forgotten. My suggestion with regard to volunteers possibly would be more properly discussed under the War Veterans Allowance Act, as the minister will tell you, but I would ask the minister at this time to consider at an early date the eligibility of the first war veteran volunteer to qualify for assistance and I recommend that the present requirement of 365 days in the United Kingdom prior to November 12, 1918 be abolished. To my mind there appears to be no just reason to distinguish between the veterans who serve voluntarily in two major wars. In Canada it actually appears to be easier to qualify allied veterans or veterans that were allies of ours during world war I than it is to qualify our own Canadian volunteers.
I now wish to discuss certain personnel of the South African force and this is one point I want to make. In some cases they arrived at the theatre of war but did not disembark prior to the cut-off date. I use the term "certain personnel" because those that are still alive, it would appear from this Pension Act and other acts covering veterans, do not qualify to be classed as veterans or to be entitled to the term "military service". Section 2(o) of the Pension Act outlines military services as service in the navy, army or air force of Canada since the commencement of world war I. With this section as it now reads it can be seen that no South African volunteer has entitlement to pension under this act, nor any service status whatsoever under the Pension Act.
An applicant who falls into this category, I understand-there are only a few of them left-must apply to the British minister of pensions. The British minister will only entertain recognition of those Canadian volunteers who landed in South Africa prior to May 31, 1902. As I said, although there are only a few of them left, Canada has made no provision to assist in any manner those South African volunteers who cannot qualify under British regulations. There is no provision under the War Veterans Allowance Act whereby assistance can be given to an early Canadian volunteer, although the need may be great. I say that somewhere in our statutes such cases should be covered. It cannot mean too much money to the Canadian taxpayers. There numbers must be less than 100.
The final point I wish to raise at this time is in connection with the monetary award that accompanies gallantry awards. Although it may not come under the heading of the Pension Act, it may have to do with the contemplated change in an administration of the act, mentioned in part 4 of the resolution, which I read previously. When we inquired

in the committee stage during the last session the reason recipients of gallantry awards in world war II received cash with their awards and those receiving the same award in world war I did not receive cash we were told that such awards in world war I were under British jurisdiction. The statement was made by the officials of the department during the 1958 session that negotiations were under way for the government of Canada to take over this jurisdiction. When agreement had been reached, it was thought that Canadians of world war I in receipt of gallantry awards would be compensated in the same manner as were those receiving the awards in world war II and since that time. Can the minister say whether those negotiations have been completed with the British ministry of pensions or other British bodies that have control of these matters? I am not quite sure whether it is the pensions ministry. I would ask the government to see that this matter is not forgotten. I would ask the minister, also, to see that the matter of the very few veterans of the South African war is not forgotten.
May I say in conclusion that I am certain every member of this house is aware of the importance of this resolution to Canada's veterans and their dependents. I hope the measure will have a successful passage through this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity to comment on the resolution concerning veterans' pensions. I should like to associate myself with the view expressed by the Minister of Veterans Affairs on introducing the resolution when, as recorded on page 735 of Hansard of December 12, 1960, he stated:
It is the desire of the people of Canada that veterans and their dependents shall receive reasonably adequate compensation.
Certainly this is the same sentiment as was expressed in slightly different terms by the subcommittee on veterans affairs set up at the recent Liberal rally, which resolved:
The Liberal party reaffirms its continued concern for Canada's veterans, believing that the country wishes to treat them in a spirit of generous gratitude for their services so readily rendered in past times of national emergency.
In my opinion veterans are patriots, and patriotism is generally defined as love for one's country. A line from one of Horace's poems runs: It is good and glorious to die for one's country. Horace lived before the birth of Christ, but even in that period patriotism was not a new thing. As a matter of fact, some 500 years before the Christian era a noble band of Spartans died a glorious death for the sake of saving their country.
But the underlying sentiment which makes men patriots is the conviction of life itself which is the most precious gift of manhood.
Pension Act
During the first world war, the second world war, or, as a matter of fact in any world war, how many patriots had we; men who left their provinces, their communities, their families, their homes and their friends and went out and fought, not for any personal distinction or any personal gain but for king and country; men who fought for their fellow countrymen so that they might live in peace and harmony without the fear of war hovering over their heads. How many veterans made the supreme sacrifice thinking they were taking part in a war to end wars? So, Mr. Chairman, let us show our gratitude to them. Let us show that they did not fight in vain. Let us show that their efforts on our behalf have been appreciated.
The principle of the resolution under discussion is, therefore, non-controversial. It is the responsibility of this government and of members of parliament irrespective of their party affiliations to see that justice is handed out to our worthy veterans. It is in this spirit that I wish to assure the minister that I shall be brief at this stage of the debate in order to expedite the introduction of the bill itself. When we have the bill in our possession we shall give it very close scrutiny, both in committee and in the standing committee on veterans affairs in order to ensure that the maximum benefit accrues to our worthy veterans.
It is, of course, unfortunate that the government was unable to bring in this legislation last year, thus complying with the plan of the former minister of veterans affairs as expressed in the issue of the Legionary of March of last year. It is unfortunate, too, that the former minister of veterans affairs, the Hon. Alfred Brooks, who no doubt worked so hard on this resolution, will not have the pleasure of guiding it through the house.
It is to be hoped that the revision in the pensions will compensate in a realistic manner for the rapid decline in the real worth of the dollar in recent years, a decline which bears heavily on those who, of necessity, have to live within the confines of an income fixed at a time when the dollar was worth a good deal more than it is today.
We welcome the provision outlined by the minister which attempts to mitigate the injustice done to those Canadian citizens who served this country well while on duty with allied forces but who do not yet receive comparable pension benefits. I share the hope so ably expressed in the speech of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that under this resolution provision will be made to place Newfoundland veterans on the same footing in connection with the payment of benefit as other Canadians. I endorse every word

Pension Act
which my hon. friend said, and urge that an attempt be made to regularize the status of Newfoundland veterans. I ask the government to take into consideration the service given by the forestry units in world war II, the merchant navy and the rescue tug service. All those who served in these bodies should be brought under the veterans' charter.
The members of the Newfoundland overseas forestry units, having answered the call of duty served side by side with the Canadian forestry corps and performed their duties in a very creditable manner. They were exposed to the same hazards as were any Canadians from any part of Canada stationed in the British isles.
It was my duty to purchase the clothing on behalf of the Newfoundland commission government for the Newfoundland forestry units prior to their departure. As far as I can understand, the foresters have never been recognized as veterans because they did not wear a uniform and were not recruited in the same way as the other fighting forces. Surely the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his colleagues will find some way to overcome this technicality and show Newfoundlanders and all Canadians that this government is not going to treat them differently from other Canadians in any of the provinces.
For several years the Newfoundlanders who served with the forestry unit have been seeking through the Canadian Legion the same recognition as is shown other Canadians who served in similar capacities. It has been stated that the commission government of Newfoundland at the time did not recognize any obligation toward the forestry unit. Surely this does not mean that the obligation did not exist and as we all know two wrongs will never make a right.
I wish to conclude by placing on the record an extract from the speech made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo as reported at page 6755 of Hansard of July 22, 1960:
I should like to express the hope that the war veterans legislation will be amended at the next session of parliament; not only that the Pension Act will be amended to permit increases in the basic pensions and to confirm and regularize the status of Newfoundland veterans, but that other veterans legislation will be amended so that the Newfoundland forestry units of world war II, the merchant navy and the members of the rescue tug service can all be brought under the veterans charter.
I hope the minister will take into consideration the brief submitted on March 31, 1960 on behalf of the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit. I ask the minister not to show any preference to the Newfoundland foresters, but to see to it that the same rule and yardstick are applied to our forces who went out and

did their work as well as they knew how, not to see that they are given any preference but to ensure that they receive the justice so well deserved.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I take this opportunity-as have hon. members who preceded me in this debate-to formally congratulate the new Minister of Veterans Affairs and wish him every success in that important portfolio. Thus far the hon. gentleman has given every indication of being a worthy successor to his predecessors.
The introduction of this resolution will be received gratefully by the various veterans organizations and by veterans generally. It has been known for some time that the government has been giving serious consideration to implementing the increases given in 1957 with a view to bringing them more in line with the recommendations made by the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations. It was expected that these increases would have been made last year and I know that it was as great a disappointment to the then minister of veterans affairs and other members of the government, as it was to all veterans, when it was decided that these benefits would have to be postponed.
That is not to say that veterans were neglected in the meantime. In fact the benefits granted by the present government make up an imposing list among which are the following: a very substantial increase in war veterans allowances; eligibility for veterans who served at least 365 days in the United Kingdom during world war I and for the widows of these veterans; reduction of the residence rule for allied veterans from 20 to 10 years; eligibility for the widows of such veterans after they have resided here for 10 years, provided their husbands would also have resided in Canada for 10 years had they lived; raising from $6,000 to $8,000 the interest a recipient may have in the property in which he resides; veterans can now receive the veterans allowance regardless of domicile under certain conditions; the repeal of the section which prohibited the payment of an allowance to an orphan receiving benefits under the Pension Act.
All of these points have been contained in resolutions advocated for many years by various veterans organizations and the amendments introduced by the government have gone a long way toward meeting these points. The abolition of the deadline for the marriage or remarriage of world war I veterans, previously advanced to 1954, enabled many veterans to claim married status.
I hope that any increases approved will include payments to those veterans who come under section 25 of the Pension Act, the

meritorious section. When the new changes recommended in this resolution are added to this list I believe we will have every reason to be happy in supporting the motion. There is, however, one matter that continues to give veterans organizations considerable concern and that is the continued practice on the part of the members of the pension commission of placing their own interpretation on section 70 of the Pension Act which reads as follows:
70. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means that it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
This concern has been expressed by various veterans organizations. It was expressed by the Canadian Legion in a resolution in the following words:
-that the government take action to ensure that the benefit of the doubt as set forth in section 70 of the Pension Act is in fact extended to all applicants under that act.
It was expressed by the army, navy and air force veterans of Canada in a resolution in these words:
Whereas the Pension Act states that in any application for pension, the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt and the adjudicating body is directed to draw all reasonable inference in favour of the applicant; and
Whereas the pension commission, the pension appeal board and medical authorities acting on their behalf, are not in many cases giving the veteran the benefit of the doubt;
Therefore be it resolved by the army, navy and air force veterans in Canada, in dominion convention assembled, that this obvious violation of the Pension Act be again called to the attention of the various bodies who adjudicate upon pension applications and that they be duly reminded of their statutory duty to give to the applicant the benefit of the doubt according to the clear and specific terms of the section above mentioned; I
I wish to place on the record some excerpts from a decision of an appeal board of the pension commission:
The doctor further stated that he agreed that the arthritic condition produced a technical difficulty in operational procedure. The board has further noted that the expert testimony adduced and contained in medical reports indicates that the pensionable condition may possibly have contributed to this veteran's death.
After a most careful and sympathetic analysis, however, of all the circumstances attendant upon death, this board can only conclude that whereas the pensionable condition may have contributed to this veteran's death the fact remains the immediate cause of death was from focal peritonitis following a gastro-enterostomy and the contributory factors cannot be considered material in this case. The advocate Mr. Harvey submitted that the medical evidence established that the pensionable condition contributed materially to death and further pointed out that although in
Pension Act
his opinion there was no doubt of this, should any doubt exist in the minds of the board it should be resolved in favour of the applicant.
The board, after carefully reviewing the entire evidence, concludes that although the possibility exists that the pensionable condition may have influenced the disease processes leading to death, the probability of such has not been sufficiently established to bring this case within the provisions of section 70.
Here is a case where the board felt there was a doubt but it was not sufficient to bring it within section 70. Many cases similar to this may be found on the files of the pension commission, the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations that maintain veterans bureaus. For many years this subject has been the subject of resolutions by these organizations based on the knowledge that as the years go by the disabilities suffered during war service, some of which were not apparent, or if they were, were not reported on discharge, would become aggravated to the extent that the ability of the veteran to earn a living was impaired. Furthermore, the difficulty of securing witnesses and evidence to substantiate their claims would increase with the passing of the years. These fears were well founded and parliament finally recognized the need and in its wisdom passed section 70 so as to remove forever the possibility that any veteran should be denied the right to compensation for any disability suffered as a result of service to his country.
The intention of parliament as set out in section 70 is clear enough; the difficulty is with the interpretation and it seems to me that members of the commission believe that the doubt mentioned means the doubt in their own minds; whereas parliament meant the doubt as to the completeness of the evidence produced on behalf of the veteran. I believe that if this matter can be cleared up, along with the addition of the new amendments, we shall be making more complete what is perhaps already the finest veterans legislation in the world.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks at this time. First of all, I should like to congratulate the new Minister of Veterans Affairs. In the few years that I have been in parliament I have come to have a tremendous respect for the members of this particular department. I believe that they are dedicated to their task, and the new minister takes over a department that I am sure is trying to do everything it can for the good of the Canadian veteran.
I should also like to pay tribute to the previous minister who not only as minister of veterans affairs but also as a veteran and a member of veterans committees over the years has done a tremendous job and has carried the torch for the veterans across

Pension Act
Canada. He has now moved on to the other place, and I trust that his good work here will bring to him the satisfaction that sometimes is the basis of many years of good health.
I want to associate myself particularly with the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. This is not the first occasion when he has taken the opportunity to make a strong plea for the Newfoundland veteran who now apparently is not receiving the same consideration as his mainland partner receives. Whatever the legal interpretation of term 38 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada may be, it is my opinion that this term should not provide food for legal argument, but every effort should be made to find some basis for granting to the Newfoundland veteran the benefits which he so rightly deserves. I would have hoped that in this legislation some consideration would be given to this particular class of veterans. We shall know in a day or so when we receive the bill what its contents are, but if this present amendment does not contain some consideration for this class of veteran I hope that any amendments which are made in the near future will give the consideration which they so justly deserve.
One coming from Newfoundland could hardly make any reference to veterans without referring to the Newfoundland forestry unit. In March of last year a delegation was received by the veterans committee, and I was particularly impressed with the brief which they presented at that time. I know that all members of this committee are keenly interested in the affairs of the Canadian veteran and I would suggest to you, and particularly to those who are members of the veterans committee, that they secure a copy of this brief and give it the thorough reading which I think it warrants.
This Newfoundland unit of foresters was formed on November 18, 1939, just a month or two after the outbreak of the second world war. It is interesting to note that some of the communications between the government of England and the commission of government of Newfoundland encouraged those people to engage themselves as foresters and to join the forestry unit rather than the regular forces. For example, on page 2 of the brief which I hold in my hand there is a reference to the encouragement which was given to those men, and in section 2 (b) we find the following:
By telegram No. 416 dated 9th November 1939 the secretary of state for dominion affairs impressed upon the Newfoundland governor the dire necessity for Newfoundland to send a labour unit immediately to the United Kingdom for the purpose of

cutting pitprops in connection with coal production in the United Kingdom which was, in his words, "vital to the war economy".
(c) The Newfoundland government felt duty bound to ask Newfoundlanders to be guided by what the United Kingdom government felt to be most advantageous for winning the war.
This leads me to believe, Mr. Chairman, that while those Newfoundlanders engaged themselves in the forestry unit, they were, at least by power of suggestion from the home office, doing what they considered to be their part in the war effort. Each individual signed a contract for the duration of the war, except for the first nine months of the war when the special contract was for six months.
It is interesting to note that in the following year, in the month of June, 1940, the contract was altered and by this change in the contract each individual had to undertake that he would not and could not be transferred to any other unit or to any of His Majesty's armed forces, and had to sign for the duration of the emergency. In other words, having been encouraged to enter the forestry unit these men were no longer free to decide whether they would or would not enter the regular forces. In reading the brief I was interested in something I found on page 7. In telegram No. 376 from the home office under date of May 16, 1940, I find the following:
Need of men skilled in forestry is so urgent that we should be grateful if recruiting organizations in Newfoundland could be advised to exercise special caution in accepting any skilled loggers as recruits for Royal Artillery Regiment.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee that these men who joined the forestry unit did so because they were encouraged to make their contribution in this direction. I feel there is an element of unfairness when these men do not receive the benefits to which in my view at least they are perfectly entitled. I hope that at some future time when the minister is considering amendments to the legislation he will give all due consideration to the plea which these men have made to the parliament of Canada through the veterans affairs committee.
When the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada were being negotiated I do not think the problem of the Newfoundland foresters was presented in the proper way. I say that for this reason. When the Newfoundland foresters were in the United Kingdom they were under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Turner. During the months preceding March, 1949, when the negotiations were going on between Newfoundland and Canada, Lieutenant Colonel Turner was sent to Ottawa to discuss the affairs of the forestry unit. Unfortunately he died en route to Ottawa. As a result the

actual facts with respect to his unit were not given serious consideration for some time, but I believe that their case has now been sufficiently well presented that parliament should give consideration to the request they have made.
Coming from a province like Newfoundland it is to be expected that I would also be particularly interested in the merchant navy and I am interested in the members of the merchant navy, not because they are a distinct class of veteran but because they are a distinct class of veteran who are not now receiving the benefits which I believe they should receive. Those of us who know the tremendous part that water transportation played in the winning of the second world war must realize that every merchant seaman was in a theatre of war and that many of them lost their lives as other veterans did on the field of battle and elsewhere. I believe that these men played a tremendous part in the victory won by the allied forces. I think they should be considered as full-time veterans and that under the Pension Act they should receive all the benefits that might accrue to a veteran of any other branch of the fighting services. I would also include the members of the rescue tug service and also the members of the fire fighter service.
I think we have come to the time in Canada when we should consider veterans legislation in the light of the contribution made and not in the light of any legal technicalities which may be the result of organizing these forces in a hurry when they were required. I say again that I am very happy to see this legislation come before the house. I know it is going to be given sympathetic consideration by members in all quarters of the house. There are parts of the legislation which will be of particular appeal not only to members of the House of Commons but to the veterans themselves. Again I would hope that on an early occasion in the future the minister will bring into the house an amendment which will give consideration to the problems that have been raised by four Newfoundland members today and I know would have been raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate who is unavoidably absent this evening. I spoke to him about the legislation a few moments ago and he assured me that he was quite in accord with the representations made by the four members from Newfoundland on this side of the house with regard to the problems of Newfoundland veterans.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks this evening on the resolution now before the house. First, I
Pension Act
should like to congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs on his appointment. We all know that he was very active with respect to veterans affairs while in the opposition as was the former minister of veterans affairs, the Hon. Mr. Brooks, who has gone to the other place. As we all know, the veterans charter was established after the second world war and it set out the various legislative items having to do with our veterans. As stated by the former minister of veterans affairs, the aim of the government when it took office in 1957 was to take the various pieces of legislation, go through them one by one and make the necessary changes by way of amendment. This has been done since that time.
It was not possible to bring about amendments with regard to disability pensions until this year and I am very glad to see that this matter is now before the house. We know what the record of the government has been. The many changes have been set out by other members who have spoken on the resolution. Changes were made in the War Veterans Allowance Act. In 1958 changes were made in soldiers' insurance and in the Veterans Insurance Act as well as in the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act.
We are glad indeed to have these changes in the Pension Act before us. Various members have spoken about different sections of the act. Some have stated that there are other changes which should be made. I am one of those who believe that the act is not perfect. There are many sections in the act which are open to different interpretations and those who practice law know that is natural. As time goes on and it is shown that changes are needed they will be made.
One was mentioned by the hon. member for Megantic when speaking on the resolution, namely section 13 (2) of the Pension Act. This

Pension Act
is one provision to which various interpretations are given by the Canadian pension commission and I believe that this section above all is one that should be clarified. As 1 have said, the government has taken action by amendments of different kinds to the various types of legislation.
I hope that the next step in this program will be changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act. We know that those who are in receipt of war veterans allowances have need of a proper amount in order to keep themselves as well as those who receive other forms of pension. No doubt the government will take this into consideration and that will be the next step in the program.
While referring to the War Veterans Allowance Act I should like to refer to a matter which has come to my attention, and no doubt to the attention of many members in this house. A veteran who is in receipt of war veterans allowance has his allowance cut when he receives the old age security pension. I believe there should be a change in this provision. There should be no cut when the veteran reaches 70 because he is entitled to his full war veterans allowance and his old age pension, just as are the other people of this country.
There was another matter mentioned by the hon. member for Swift Surrent-Maple Creek when he spoke this afternoon and that was the regulation concerning veterans who served in the first world war. As we all know they must have served 365 days prior to November 12, 1918. I feel that there should be a change in this regulation because the number of first world war veterans is getting less all the time. I believe there should be a reduction in the number of days. In my own constituency I know of a case, and no doubt many other hon. members have similar cases in their constituencies, of a war veteran who really needs help but who is seven days short of having served the required number of days.
There was a matter mentioned by the chairman of our veterans committee. Incidentally he does a wonderful job. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton referred to the possibility of setting up an appeal section in the Canadian pension commission. As I understood him he meant that it would be a section which would deal with appeals from the Canadian pension commission and from the appeal board in the same manner as our appellate court. I believe that this would be a good step in dealing with some of these cases.
Finally, the hon. member for Trinity-Conception spoke this evening and dealt with the new platform of the Liberal party, as a result of this last rally, as it related to the 
veteran. He said this indicated the concern of the Liberal party for the veteran. I should like to say that concern for the veteran is also shown by the government and evidence of that concern is the many changes which have taken place in the three and a half years during which we have been in power.
Finally, I understand that after second reading the bill will be sent to the veterans affairs committee, at which time we will be able to go into the matter fully. We are all looking forward, as members of the committee, to investigating the various matters affecting the veterans of this country. May I again join with those who have commended and supported this resolution which is now before us.

speechtext:

In passing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity of paying tribute to the Canadian Legion. Over the years, by sound leadership and dedicated service, the Legion has established itself as the mouthpiece of the veteran. One could point to the number of projects that they have sponsored. This evening, in the time at my disposal, I should like to especially commend the outstanding work being done by the service bureau. I have found this bureau particularly helpful since I came to Ottawa as a member of parliament, inasmuch as they have helped me in every way possible in resolving a number of contentious cases.
I think it is interesting to observe that along with the appointment of the new minister there have been other changes. For instance, a new chairman of the war veterans allowance board has been appointed in the person of Colonel Bill Cromb. He is well and favourably known across western Canada for his work with veterans, first as superintendent of welfare with the D.V.A. at Edmonton, subsequently as district administrator at Edmonton and Winnipeg and finally as regional administrator for the western provinces.
Then also, about a year ago there was a change in the chairmanship of the pension commission, in the person of Mr. Anderson. The comparatively new chairman came to the commission with a wealth of experience in veterans affairs inasmuch as he was previously secretary of the Canadian Legion. Moreover, other changes have been made in the pension commission and in the war veterans allowance board by way of superannuation.
What does all this mean? If we are to follow the usual pattern that is exercised in life-and I say this with no reflection on the past administration-I think this means new ideas. I think it means a different approach in the administration of these two acts which I maintain are complementary one to the other.
Mr. Chairman, if you combine this new administration with the proposed amendments,
Pension Act
and the fact that our world war I veterans are on the average about 70 years of age, I think it is reasonable to contemplate that a more liberal interpretation of the Pension Act in certain areas and the War Veterans Allowance Act could be expected.
As one who has been in close contact with veterans for a number of years and who is quite well acquainted with many of their problems, I want to say this. It is one thing to make a serviceman out of a civilian, but it is quite difficult to adjust back into civilian life. Notwithstanding the fact that Canada, as has been stated previously today, has a rehabilitation plan that is second to none in the world, there are a number of servicemen who find it extremely difficult to adjust themselves back into civilian life. This is something that should never be lost sight of by all Canadians. The success of a serviceman being rehabilitated back into civilian life depends upon a number of factors such as, for example, his age; his education on enlistment; his length of service and type of service, combat or otherwise; the environment to which he returns, such as his parents and family; and, most of all, down to the ground, right from the heart interest and understanding by the public at large, particularly the community to which he returns.
While this resolution will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs where it will be discussed in detail, there are a few observations I should like to make. The first one is with regard to the method by which applications for pensions are received. If I follow the procedure correctly, the pension commission first refers the submission for entitlement to the medical advisory branch. In turn a report is made by a doctor with his opinion. Following this the policy that is laid down is that two or more members of the pension commission must adjudicate on the pension claim.
The question that arises in my mind is this, particularly in view of the department report for the fiscal year 1958-59 indicating that approximately 50 per cent of pension commission hearings were successful on appeal. Does the pension commission depend too much on the opinion expressed by the medical adviser? There may be an answer to this question, but on the face of the matter it would appear to mean that more time and study should be given to boardroom decisions.
In all fairness, I should add that when a case is appealed the commissioners have an opportunity to meet the witnesses and to assess the over-all value of the testimony. Be that as it may, in the few cases that have come to my notice the appeals, by and large,

Pension Act
are successful on the same evidence by which the commission had previously ruled adversely.
My second observation is on the composition of the appeal boards which travel across the country. Originally the idea was that the board would be balanced; that is to say, a board would comprise one doctor, one lawyer and one layman, with the present composition of the present commission it is contended that a board comprised of two doctors with a layman or a lawyer, attaches too much weight to the medical aspects of the case.
My third observation is in connection with that common complaint which has been raised several times today-I refer to the interpretation of section 70-wherein it is contended that the pension commission relies to a great extent on the medical advisers and that, notwithstanding the weight of evidence in favour of the applicant, the benefits of this section cannot be resolved until a doubt has been created in the minds of the commissioners.
As has been stated here previously, I do not think there is much we can do to amend the act. After all, you can make an act and you can make regulations and they are just as good as is the administration. I am not complaining of the administration. I think the position in which the pension commissioners are placed by this section 70 is an extremely difficult one. The question arises whether or not they give the applicant the benefit of the doubt is debatable.
My fourth observation is with regard to pension advocates.

subtopic: BAGGAGE AND PASSENGER FACILITIES, DORVAL AIRPORT
BAGGAGE AND PASSENGER FACILITIES, DORVAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of Transport (a) entered into any agreements; (b) issued any charters, to persons, organizations, or companies, for the purpose of handling baggage and/or transporting of passengers at Montreal airport, Dorval?
2.	If so: (a) what are the names of the persons, companies or organizations? (b) on what dates were these charters or agreements instituted? (c) what is the content of each agreement or charter?
3.	Have any changes been made in any charter or agreement since it was instituted?
4.	If so, what was the change made, its purpose, and the date?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
1.	(a) Yes, for transporting passengers; (b) other than entering into the agreement under (a) the department does not issue charters. Charters for public transportation facilities are issued by the Quebec provincial transportation board.
2.	(a) Murray Hill Limousine Service Limited; (b) the limousine concession with Murray Hill dates back to August 1, 1947, but at that time the company's name was Murray Hill Taxis Limited; (c) the agreement contains the clauses and conditions outlining the terms of the agreement, such as the period for which the agreement was granted, the payments to be made under the agreement and other clauses considered in the public interest.
3 and 4. The payment under the original agreement of August 1, 1947, was $7,200 per annum. The rental was increased, effective August 1, 1951, to $9,360 per annum. The rental was again increased, effective August 1, 1952, to $12,000 per annum.
An agreement has been renegotiated and submitted for approval whereby the department is to receive $50,000 per annum effective December 1, 1960, for a period of five years, with the rental to be reviewed again thereafter.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS IN B.C. DUE TO FLOODS
speechtext:
1.	For how many days was service on the main line of the Canadian National Railways discontinued to Vancouver because of recent floods in British Columbia?
2.	(a) How many men were at least temporarily laid oil by the Canadian National Railways as a result of this break in service? (b) how many of these men have since been re-employed? (c) when does the Canadian National Railways expect to re-employ all who were laid off as a result of this emergency?
3.	Were any of these men offered alternative employment in the task of restoring the disrupted service, if not, for what reason?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
The management of the Canadian National Railways advise as follows:-
1.	Fourteen days. Service was disrupted January 15 and restored January 29.
2.	(a) Two hundred and seventeen; (b) as of January 31 all re-employed; (c) answered by (b).
3.	The employees involved were members of the mechanical and car departments. They were laid off because no trains were operating and no alternate work was available. Work rules of the craft organizations involved excludes the transfer of employees between crafts to exercise seniority or perform work belonging to another craft.
